It's the time of year when the IRS and state tax agencies send out notices for additional taxes, missed payments, and other tax challenges.

If you've ever received one, you've probably noticed that the amount due can have three components: tax, interest, and penalties.

Here's something I've mentioned on the podcast over the years that has saved members of the ChooseFI community real money: You can ask to have certain tax penalties removed. The IRS calls this penalty abatement.

According to recent reports, in fact, the IRS now automatically waives some penalties for eligible taxpayers with a good compliance history. But if you receive a notice assessing a penalty, I think it's worth requesting relief.

Show of every Jan van Eyck portrait reveals many newly introduced sides to his works

💡 Key Takeaways

  • But we stand to know a lot more about him this month, when London’s National Gallery brings together all nine of his surviving panel portraits along with his lone surviving drawing, also a portrait.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there is a lot we do not know for certain about Jan van Eyck, including where and when he was born. What we do know is that his career—from the early 1420s until his death in 1441—helped launch the Early Netherlandish school, influencing the use of oil paint far beyond his native Low Countries and instilling a newly introduced and arguably everlasting value of verisimilitude in Western art.

But we stand to know a lot more about him this month, when London’s National Gallery brings together all nine of his surviving panel portraits along with his lone surviving drawing, also a portrait. The bijoux blockbuster show will give scholars a unique opportunity to compare scattered works of singular importance. Van Eyck: The Portraits—with a checklist that expands all the way to 13 through the addition of three works on paper by his followers—is built around some remarkable pairings.

Fresh from a conservation treatment completed in 2024, the National Gallery’s own Portrait of a Man (Self-Portrait?) (1433) will meet up with Portrait of Margaret van Eyck (1439), the artist’s wife, on loan from Bruges, where Van Eyck had his workshop when he was the court painter to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy.

The National Gallery’s Arnolfini Portrait (1434), Van Eyck’s enigmatic view of an elegantly dressed couple in an impressive reception room, will be shown for the first time with its related work from the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin clearly showing the same man, Portrait of a Man (Giovanni Arnolfini?) (around 1435-38).

Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum is loaning Portrait of an Elderly Man (A Scholar?) (around 1438). It will be shown with the preparatory drawing from Dresden, in goldpoint and silverpoint on prepared paper, with its revealing notes on how to colour the painting itself.

Van Eyck’s devotional portraits, such as those in his groundbreaking Ghent Altarpiece and the Musée du Louvre’s recently treated Madonna of Chancellor Rolin (around 1435), are outside the scope of the National Gallery exhibition.

Some of the portraits have reverse imagery of fictive marble, and the museum is placing them in cases so visitors can view both sides. “We’re really excited to be able to show people how amazing the reverse is,” states Nicholas Flory, who is curating the show along with Emma Capron, the museum’s curator of early Netherlandish and German painting. Flory says the elaborate reverses suggest that “these objects were not designed for a single kind of specific space or to be flat against the wall”, but rather “to be interacted with”.

Newness abounds in the show. The Arnolfini Portrait had long had an ornate Gothic Revival frame until it was replaced in 2024 by a 15th-century gilded frame. Meanwhile, the Berlin work, showing its male figure in distinctive red chaperon headgear, completed a conservation treatment in 2023 that removed distorting yellow varnish. The result of that treatment, states Stephan Kemperdick, the curator of Netherlandish paintings before 1600 at the Gemäldegalerie, has been to “make the palette cooler”. Before, he says, the chaperon was “fire-engine red”, and the man’s face looked “suntanned”, whereas now, he says, the face is “pinkish or whiteish—a feature that distinguished people from the better classes in the 15th century”.

Recent findings suggest that the London exhibition, which Kemperdick calls a “once-in-a-lifetime” event, is a culmination of sorts. Several Van Eyck works, including the Ghent Altarpiece, have undergone recent treatments, which Flory says has been “an impetus in Van Eyck scholarship”, and the National Gallery show reflects new research into Van Eyck’s technique, his original frames and inscriptions. Recent analysis of the National Gallery’s self-portrait, examined during its recent treatment, revealed how Van Eyck modulated the blueness of the background in the lower-right corner to “throw the sitter’s shoulder forward”, Flory says, creating a 3D effect.

According to recent reports, just out of view of the show itself, lurking in Kemperdick’s catalogue essay, is a possible bombshell: that the couple shown in the Arnolfini Portrait are not the titular Italian merchant and his wife at all, but rather Van Eyck and his wife. This would also mean that the Gemäldegalerie’s Portrait of a Man (Giovanni Arnolfini?) is also a self-portrait.

Recent findings suggest that the Arnolfini Portrait is among the gallery’s most popular works, and the minuscule size of the show is in marked contrast with the likely museumgoer interest. However, Flory says the diminutive roster is, in fact, the big attraction.

“There was the possibility to expand it beyond Van Eyck and show his work in the context of his contemporaries,” Flory indicates. “But because he is such a monumental figure in the history of Western painting, and his portraits are so special, we really wanted to focus the exhibition on just Van Eyck himself.” Luckily, he adds, the remarkable loans, which have involved several museums sending some of their most precious works, mean “we got everything we were hoping for”.

• Jan van Eyck: The Portraits, National Gallery, London, 21 November-11 April 2027.

Tech Report: Letting the Film Breathe: A Conversation with Filmmaker Julie Bayer Salzman

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2884 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2013, Julie Bayer Salzman’s five-year-old son came home from kindergarten talking about his prefrontal cortex and his amygdala.
  • Sources indicate that just Breathe grew into Mindful Shorts, an ongoing series of experiential documentaries that follow mindfulness across the life span.
  • According to recent reports, former Mindful editor Ava Whitney-Coulter first spoke with Salzman in 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2013, Julie Bayer Salzman’s five-year-old son came home from kindergarten talking about his prefrontal cortex and his amygdala. She was so struck that she signed up for the same mindfulness course his school used to train its teachers. During one of her meditations, she pictured a short film. That film became Just Breathe, in which elementary school kids describe how mindfulness helps them work with anger. It was featured on Oprah’s Super Soul Sunday and has since been translated into six languages and shown in classrooms around the world.

Sources indicate that just Breathe grew into Mindful Shorts, an ongoing series of experiential documentaries that follow mindfulness across the life span. The five films so far cover anger in childhood, anxiety in middle school, depression in high school, addiction in midlife, and grief in the elder years. Made with her husband and creative partner, cinematographer Josh Salzman, through their company Wavecrest Films, the series is funded by donations and offered free to anyone who needs it.

According to recent reports, former Mindful editor Ava Whitney-Coulter first spoke with Salzman in 2024. After the recent release of Bayer’s latest film, Broken & Beautiful, Mindful Chief Editor Siri Myhrom caught up with her at her home in LA. They spoke about what it’s like to work on creative projects with her partner, what advertising taught her, how her practice shows up on set, and what she’s learned from the people at the heart of her newest films.

It has been revealed that siri Myhrom: You spent more than a decade producing commercial campaigns before directing your own work. What did advertising teach you about storytelling, and what did you have to unlearn?

Julie Bayer Salzman: Advertising taught me the importance of strong visuals in nonfiction filmmaking. Sometimes documentary filmmakers don’t place as much value on the visual style as they do on simply capturing the action unfolding in order to tell the best story, and of course that makes a lot of sense in some respect, because story is everything; however, film is a visual medium, and a documentary needs to be more than journalistic. It’s worth taking time to capture reality as beautifully as you can. That said, sometimes when documentaries look too slick, it can be a distraction. To me it’s vital to find the balance.

We ask ourselves a simple question: What kind of value does it add to our shared human experience on this planet?

Recent findings suggest that commercials also taught me how to distill a story to its essence in a short amount of time. And yet, taken too far, that can be a detriment to any story. I had to unlearn to some extent the tendency to truncate a scene out of learned impatience, or playing into the audience’s short attention span. I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but there is not a lot of breathing space in a commercial!

This may seem corny or cliché, but when I started practicing mindfulness, I actually started to lean more into the idea of allowing a film to breathe. As I was learning to breathe more consciously myself, my filmmaking style started to evolve differently, more experientially—slowing the pace, and allowing more pauses between the thoughts or statements.

It has been revealed that SM: Wavecrest’s mission is to make content with a positive social impact, and you’ve said you choose projects carefully so you don’t add to the noise. How do you decide whether a project is worth making?

Recent findings suggest that JBS: We ask ourselves a simple question: What kind of value does it add to our shared human experience on this planet? Meaning: Does the project help us evolve collectively? Change the way we see the world? Inspire us to be better humans? Cultivate connection with nature or other humans? Laugh? If none of those things, then we’ll pass, thanks.

SM: You and Josh are married as well as creative partners. How do you divide the work, and how do you handle creative disagreements?

In a recent development, JBS: We’re incredibly lucky to have very complementary skill sets, while often sharing feelings as well as values. I’m big-picture; he’s details. I’ve got a million ideas and my antennae up at all times, taking in everything around me. I “see” the film conceptually, and have my producer skill set from years in commercials, therefore I tend to take the lead as director and producer; but he’s the cinematographer, and I trust him implicitly to capture my vision in the best possible way.

I can’t say we have creative disagreements, because honestly, we don’t. We respect each other’s strengths in a really beautiful way. It’s a unique creative synergy that I do not take for granted.

Recent findings suggest that when it’s time to edit, I lay out the story, then pass it to him to sculpt the fine details that I usually have no patience for, like on which exact frame to place a cut. He enjoys tedium in a way I don’t.

Industry observers note that I can’t say we have creative disagreements, because honestly, we don’t. We respect each other’s strengths in a really beautiful way. It’s a unique creative synergy that I do not take for granted.

SM: When did mindfulness become part of your personal life, and when did you realize it could be the subject of your films?

Industry observers note that JBS: Mindfulness became part of my life when my son started kindergarten in 2013. He came home at the age of five, talking about his prefrontal cortex and his amygdala, thanks to the social-emotional learning curriculum at his school, and I immediately enrolled in the course that the school’s principal used to train the teachers. While meditating one day, I envisioned the first film in the Mindful Shorts series, Just Breathe, and promptly made that film. Once I saw the success it was having, I realized that people were hungry for this type of learning, and the rest of the series evolved from there.

It has been revealed that SM: You describe the Mindful Shorts as “experiential” films. What does that mean to you, and how do you design a film that viewers experience rather than just watch?

In a recent development, JBS: It means artfully crafting a film that results more in an embodied experience for the audience, rather than a passive viewing. We don’t conform to traditional standards in order to tell a story; we shape it in such a way that we hope the viewers walk away from the film feeling different energetically than they did at the start. That there is an actual impact on the nervous system—a sense of calm, of understanding—a certain kind of peace within.

When I’m interviewing people, I rarely consult my list of predetermined interview questions. Instead, I like to have a more intimate conversation, where the responses lead to more questions, rather than just asking questions in search of answers.

SM: Does your own mindfulness practice change how you behave on set, such as how you listen, when you stay quiet, or how you handle the unexpected?

Industry observers note that JBS: Absolutely. The quality of presence, of attention, are much greater now. I’m far less in my head than I used to be, and it allows for more spontaneity and creative problem solving. I think my practice allows me to be much more fluid and present than I used to be.

When I’m interviewing people, I rarely consult my list of predetermined interview questions. Instead, I like to have a more intimate conversation, where the responses lead to more questions, rather than just asking questions in search of answers. The goal is not to cross items off a list; it’s to have an experience with the process itself.

SM: Mindfulness is an inner experience, and film is a visual medium. How do you show something that happens inside a person?

According to recent reports, JBS: When you’re talking about something in one’s interior world, the exterior world must match it. Yes, film itself is a visual medium, but filmmaking as an art form is multisensory. In addition to having a distinct visual style, we place an enormous value on sound—ambient noise, music, everything—as well as on editorial pacing. It all must reflect the emotional tone behind what is being said, the changes and transformation that a character is going through when they are learning how to mindfully show up in the world.

We are not intimidating folks; I think we are warm and open by nature.

SM: Your films are unscripted and often feature people talking about very personal struggles. How do you create the kind of safety and trust that lets people be that open on camera?

Recent findings suggest that JBS: I’m not sure I can answer this question, because it’s not something I consciously do. I think it’s mostly inherent to who both Josh and I are as human beings. We are not intimidating folks; I think we are warm and open by nature. I like to think that people just instinctively trust that we are safe to be vulnerable with, that we emanate an air of security.

SM: The series follows mindfulness from childhood through old age, moving from anger, to anxiety, depression, addiction, and grief. Was that structure planned from the beginning, or did it develop as you went?

JBS: Both. After the success of Just Breathe (on anger and elementary school kids), I recognized there was more work to be done. I awoke at 3 a.m., seeing the rest of the series in my head, so I grabbed my journal, sat on the couch, and wrote the progression of the films in a way that made sense to me.

What’s after elementary school? Middle school, when we start to name “stress.” I immediately thought about how people tend to project their anxieties on the world around them, and decided we had to project images on our subjects for that film (which eventually became Release). And then I started to think about high school, when we start to name “Depression,” and I began conjuring up what that film (Into Light) might look like. Next I started to think about the stage of middle life, when addiction tends to surface and become a problem for many. And on and on…it was a middle-of-the-night revelation of sorts.

In a recent development, the two most recent Mindful Shorts carry the series into adulthood. A Good Day (32 minutes) explores mindfulness and addiction in midlife, and won at the Real HeArt Film Festival. Broken & Beautiful (23 minutes) centers on Sandy Phillips, who turned to mindfulness after the death of her daughter, and took top honors at LA Shorts.

SM: A Good Day takes on addiction in midlife and is the longest Mindful Short so far. Why did this subject need more time than the earlier films?

In a recent development, JBS: Addiction is often the result of the unprocessed experiences that the earlier films delve into (anger, anxiety, depression, and trauma), and it’s something we don’t often deal with until we’re middle aged, so as I was editing the film, I felt the need to go deeper into it, covering ground I thought was necessary in order to be more comprehensive, which naturally resulted in a longer film. I guess it’s fair to say that the topic itself seemed to dictate the length of the film.

When you’re young, a loss (like a breakup with a first love, for example) seems like the end of the world, but older people know it’s just one of many, and that life is full of losses.

In a recent development, SM: Broken & Beautiful is about a particular kind of grief, the terrible loss of a child, and, more generally, grief in the elder years. What did you learn from older subjects about presence and loss that younger subjects couldn’t have taught you?

It has been revealed that JBS: When you’re young, a loss (like a breakup with a first love, for example) seems like the end of the world, but older people know it’s just one of many, and that life is full of losses. The subject of Broken & Beautiful, Sandy Phillips, possesses a certain wisdom that only comes with age. That’s not to say that someone younger couldn’t speak to loss or grief, but she has lived through so much—and she started practicing mindfulness specifically to help herself process and navigate the death of her daughter.

In a recent development, that kind of perspective is rarely inherent in any one person’s being; it takes real time and intention to cultivate and embody it. Her particular quality of presence and attention is something that is earned, and learned, over years.

SM: Did making Broken & Beautiful affect how you deal with grief in your own life?

It has been revealed that JBS: I think it impacted Josh more than me so far, as he had to deal with the unexpected death of his mother from a heart attack in 2012—a trauma that took him a long time to process. I think I can speak for him, though, when I say he no longer sees death as an ending to a person or the relationship with that person—something that was very difficult for him to accept earlier.

Industry observers note that and then, sadly and tragically, the young kintsugi artist in Broken & Beautiful, Fumika Tanokashira, died suddenly last spring (2026), and I’m not sure I can quite put my finger on it but there was something profound about it all—the fact that she is the one showing us metaphorically, via kintsugi, how to put our lives back together after a terrible loss, and here she is the one now gone. It just leaves me speechless every time I think about it.

For some people, anecdotes are insufficient, and I understand why.

It has been revealed that SM: Your next film is about trauma in young adults and will focus on the science behind mindfulness. Why add a scientific angle now, and how do you plan to balance research with personal stories?

In a recent development, JBS: I haven’t been awoken by a vision for that one yet! But I trust it will come…it always does. Sometimes it’s imagined ahead of time; sometimes it just emerges organically during the process of making a film. We shall see what the future holds.

But to answer the question of “why add a scientific angle now”: because skeptics still exist. For some people, anecdotes are insufficient, and I understand why. Proof must be in the data. Well, there’s plenty of data out there, and I intend to do something with it. I just have to find the right people who wish to collaborate on making that film. I know they’re out there.

In a recent development, SM: The Mindful Shorts are funded through donations and offered for free. What does that model make possible, and what does it make harder?

Sources indicate that JBS: What the model makes possible is grant money, because the series is produced as not-for-profit. We also retain full ownership and creative control of the content. There’s a certain satisfaction in knowing that anyone who needs the films can access them for free, even if it takes years to find them!

Sources indicate that yet the downside of that all is that we don’t have access to “investor” money. Investors want to know they’ll get their money back and more (spoiler alert: they won’t). It’s also harder to get third-party distribution when you go the not-for-profit model, so we self-distribute on YouTube, Vimeo, and other social media platforms (as well as of course have the films up on our website, Wavecrest Films). It’s certainly not the most lucrative way of doing things, but it feels right given the nature of what we’re trying to do.

Everything stems from awareness. Without real personal growth on a larger societal level, the Earth will continue to suffer.

SM: You’ve urged your audience to work on being better humans because the planet demands it. How do your environmental work and your mindfulness work connect for you?

JBS: Our first film, Time & Tide (2006), was on climate change in the South Pacific, and for years afterward, the environment was top on our list of topics we felt we, as filmmakers, must address. But then I started to think that there was no point trying to convince people to change their actions without teaching them first about self-awareness.

Everything stems from awareness. Without real personal growth on a larger societal level, the Earth will continue to suffer. We have to heal ourselves first if we wish to heal the planet. I do firmly believe though that once there’s a larger sea change of consciousness, planetary health will improve—one person at a time.

Sources indicate that siri Liv Myhrom is a writer, editor, and certified spiritual director from Minneapolis, MN, where she has lived with her husband and two young daughters for 20 years. Her meditation practices include cycling, cold dipping in the nearby lake, and playing the ukulele (low skill but lots of gusto). She is the Editor at Mindful.

Why Accessibility Is An Operational Capability, Not A Feature

📅 2026-06-30 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2222 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mikhail Prosmitskiy is a Software Engineer who loves making complex things feel simple — and fast.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mikhail Prosmitskiy is a Software Engineer who loves making complex things feel simple — and fast. He’s spent years building everything from crypto … More about Mikhail ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

It has been revealed that we know that right now, a senior engineer is shipping a checkout flow they “built” in a single afternoon. AI assistant does the heavy lifting, happy path runs clean, and a rotating chevron spins on the order summary. Two weeks later, engineering gets a notice from customer support: a blind customer using a screen reader can’t complete the purchase because the “Pay Now” control is a with a click handler. No role. Not focusable. Not working.

In a recent development, that gap — between code that runs and a product people can actually use — is becoming one of the defining engineering challenges of the AI era. Teams can generate UI faster than ever, but they still have to guarantee that what they ship is usable, secure, and maintainable.

Accessibility sits right in the middle of that problem.

According to recent reports, this is not an article about compliance checklists or end-of-project audits. It’s about engineering systems. Specifically, why accessibility should be treated as an operational capability — alongside privacy, security, reliability, and observability — and what that looks like in practice.

For years, the default way to “do” accessibility was the one-time, audit-only approach: hire a firm, get a list of 200 findings, fix some of them, file the report. A lot of teams have now moved beyond this model — and the reason is worth looking into.

Recent findings suggest that audits do matter. For sales, procurement, governance — they’re essential. When a buyer asks for a VPAT or an ACR, you need one. When legal asks if you’re meeting requirements, you need documentation. Audits serve those purposes well.

According to recent reports, but audits don’t help you build accessible features during sprint planning. Audits can cost points during a sprint. They don’t catch problems before merge requests. They don’t scale with deployment velocity. The mistake, essentially, is tackling accessibility as a snapshot when you really need constant monitoring. Six months after the audit, the product has shipped dozens of releases, multiple upcoming features, and a redesigned nav. The report is now fiction. Compliance is not a state you reach — it’s a state you maintain, and complexity fights you the whole way.

It has been revealed that the WebAIM Million report, which scans the top one million home pages every year, found that 95.9% of pages had detectable WCAG failures in its 2026 run, with an average of 56.1 errors per page. The number of page elements jumped more than 20% in a single year, likely driven by AI-enabled development and ‘vibe coding’ — and more elements mean more places to break. Accessibility debt behaves exactly like technical debt: every inaccessible component you ship becomes a future remediation project, and the interest compounds.

Any strategy that treats accessibility as a periodic event rather than a continuous property of the system is going to lose.

With the scale at which teams now generate UI, the gap doesn’t just persist; it multiplies.

Industry observers note that start with how fast this arrived. In February 2025, Andrej Karpathy coined “vibe coding” — a way of working where you “fully give in to the vibes” and “forget that the code even exists”. You describe intent, the model generates, you accept the diffs without reading them. It was meant for weekend projects. It did not stay there. Y Combinator reported that 25% of its Winter 2025 batch had codebases that were 95% AI-generated.

Models don’t land on non-semantic markup by accident — three forces push them there. Most React code on GitHub uses non-semantic “soup”, so that’s what the models learn. Human reviewers and evaluators judge output visually, so the feedback loop rewards looks, not semantics. And is fewer tokens than , so absent a constraint, the model takes the cheap path.

Here’s the thing about AI-generated UI: it’s inaccessible by default. Not occasionally — by default. A developer writing in Frontend Masters tested AI-generated React components across multiple tools and documented the pattern. A typical AI-generated sidebar had ten distinct accessibility failures in twenty-nine lines: no landmark, no heading, no list structure, elements with click handlers instead of buttons, no aria-expanded, no keyboard handling, and unlabeled icons. The accessibility tree — the structure screen readers actually read — came back as flat, unstructured text. “Same pixels” as the author put it. “One is a door. The other is a painting of a door”.

Now connect this to security, because the two failures come from the same root. Veracode’s 2025 GenAI Code Security Report tested large language models across dozens of coding tasks and found that a large fraction of AI-generated code introduced security vulnerabilities — including OWASP Top 10 flaws. Cross-site scripting failures were particularly common, and security performance did not meaningfully improve with newer, larger models. The problem wasn’t model intelligence. It was process: developers generating code without specifying security constraints and accepting output without systematic verification.

It has been revealed that the same shortcut that skips the security review skips the accessibility review. At scale, AI won’t close the accessibility gap — it has industrialized the very thing that creates it.

The fix is not to ban AI. Your developers are already using it. The fix is to constrain it and verify it — to treat AI as a very fast teammate who always needs guardrails.

This is usually where someone states, “Guardrails? Sounds great, but they will slow us down.”.

In practice, the opposite tends to be true.

Sources indicate that shift-left is the entire DevOps thesis, and it applies cleanly here. An accessibility issue caught during design review is a comment. The same issue found in production is a remediation project.

Industry observers note that catching an accessibility concern as a component is built takes minutes. Fixing one after the fact — discovering it in an audit, diagnosing the root cause, restructuring the markup, applying the necessary fix, writing tests — can easily take hours. Multiply that across hundreds of findings from a late-stage audit, and you have weeks of unplanned work that earlier automated checks — whether in design reviews, development workflows, or CI — could have prevented.

Recent findings suggest that teams that integrate accessibility into everyday workflows avoid the expensive surprises: emergency audits, remediation sprints, procurement blockers, and redesigns that quietly break core user journeys. Accessibility doesn’t reduce velocity. Unexpected work reduces velocity. In-flow accessibility is one way of eliminating unexpected work.

The organizations that scale accessibility successfully do not rely on heroes. They rely on systems.

In a recent development, the highest-leverage place to start is the design system. One accessible component can be reused thousands of times. The GOV.UK Design System is a useful example: components undergo both automated and manual testing using assistive technologies such as JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver, and TalkBack. The team is explicit about the limits of automation and supplements tooling with user testing involving people with disabilities. They’re equally clear that using the design system doesn’t “magically” make a service accessible; it just gives you a higher starting point.

It has been revealed that accessibility becomes infrastructure. That’s the lesson.

From there, it moves into the engineering workflow:.

Finally, accessibility becomes enforceable through automation:.

Industry observers note that at that point, accessibility stops depending on memory and starts depending on the process. It becomes part of your platform.

A few implementation patterns consistently show up in teams that do this well.

Instead of fixing accessibility after generation, bake requirements directly into tooling through Cursor rules, Copilot instructions, or repository-level standards. Tell the model to use semantic HTML. Tell it when to use buttons versus links. Tell it to expose the state and labels correctly. Models follow persistent constraints far more reliably than one-off prompts.

Sources indicate that comboboxes, menus, tabs, modals, and similar controls routinely become accessibility hotspots. Libraries such as Radix UI, React Aria, and Headless UI already solve many of these problems. The scalable approach is not about repeatedly implementing accessibility correctly. It’s inheriting accessible behavior from well-tested primitives.

Focus order, labels, heading hierarchy, and interaction states should be specified before implementation begins. If accessibility requirements are absent from the design artifact, they are often absent from the final product. A simple memo at design handoff — what is the tab order, what are the labels, what happens on error — removes a huge amount of guesswork later.

Recent findings suggest that none of these patterns is exotic. They’re just DevOps and platform thinking applied to accessibility.

Engineering leaders rarely prioritize accessibility solely because of regulations. But regulations, procurement requirements, user retention, and product quality all point in the same direction.

It has been revealed that legal pressure continues to increase. Digital accessibility lawsuits in the United States have stayed in the thousands per year, and they are not limited to large enterprises. The European Accessibility Act is now enforceable across the EU, applying to e‑commerce, banking, ticketing, telecoms, and more, regardless of where the company is headquartered. The message is clear: accessibility is no longer a “nice-to-have” in the eyes of regulators.

It has been revealed that but compliance is only part of the story. The bigger story is the market you leave on the table. The World Economic Forum (December 2023) estimates that the world’s 1.3 billion people with disabilities, “along with their friends and family, has a spending power of $13 trillion”; disabled consumers alone control roughly $8 trillion in annual disposable income, per the Valuable 500.

In a recent development, in the UK alone, the Click-Away Pound Report 2019 found the “Click-Away Pound has risen to £17.1 billion” — more than 4.9 million users with access needs who abandon inaccessible sites and spend elsewhere, up almost 45% from £11.75 billion in 2016. People don’t file a bug report. They leave and buy from a competitor.

Recent findings suggest that there is also a procurement reality that turns accessibility from a cost into a moat. If you sell B2B or to government, you will increasingly be asked for proof of accessibility — VPATs/ACRs or equivalent documentation. According to Level Access’s Seventh Annual State of Digital Accessibility Report, 75% of organizations now require proof of accessibility at least most of the time when purchasing digital products — essentially unchanged from 74% in the previous report, but with a notable shift towards stricter enforcement, as those that always require it rose from 27% to 31%. A strong ACR accelerates the sales cycle; a weak one, or none at all, creates redlines that stall or kill it. For some buyers, this is a hard requirement before your product can even enter evaluation. A strong accessibility story accelerates the sales cycle. A weak one creates redlines that stall or kill it.

In a recent development, step back and the deeper pattern is clear: accessibility is a proxy for engineering maturity. A team that ships semantic HTML, manages focus, exposes state correctly, and tests it in CI is a team that has its house in order. The same discipline that produces an accessible component produces a maintainable, testable, less buggy one.

For dev and product leaders, that’s the real business case: accessibility work is platform work. It pays off every time a feature ships faster and more smoothly, with less rework, than it otherwise would have.

In a recent development, if you take one thing from this, make it this: accessibility doesn’t come from an audit, a hero, or a heroic remediation sprint before launch. It comes from systems.

An accessible design system so components start right. A Definition of Done so they stay right. Automated testing and CI gates so regressions fail the build. Governance, so someone owns it. Guardrails for AI-assisted development so your fastest tool stops being your biggest liability.

None of those practices is particularly glamorous. That’s exactly why they work. They’re the same kinds of boring, reliable systems you already trust for security, reliability, and performance.

Industry observers note that but there’s one thing no tool on that list can do. No linter, no automated scanner run, no dashboard will ever tell you what it’s actually like to use your product as a blind person with a screen reader, or to navigate your checkout with a keyboard because a tremor makes a mouse inoperable. So build the systems — you need them, and they’re the only way accessibility survives contact with a real release schedule. But test with real users with disabilities regularly. The first time you sit behind someone using JAWS to fight through a form your team thought was “done”, something changes. The tooling tells you whether you passed. A real person tells you whether it actually works.

It has been revealed that accessibility is not a feature. It’s an operational capability. Treat it that way, and you get something dev and product leaders already care about: a faster, safer, more reliable way to ship software.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Asante regalia gold objects on loan from the British Museum and Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) will remain on show in Kumasi, Ghana until 2030 following the extension of loan agreements by the two UK museums. The British Museum has loaned 15 objects while the V&A lent 17 pieces, almost all of which were looted during military operations in the late 19th century.

The British Museum and the V&A signed a loan agreement in 2024 with Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, the 16th Asantehene (King of the Asante), to return the gold regalia to the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi, the historic capital of what was then the Asante (Ashanti) empire. The loans will be renewed for a further three years at the end of the current term in April 2027. The two UK museums are legally unable to deaccession so the objects are being returned as long-term loans.

“The rollover of the loan agreement was always likely and from both the British Museum’s and Manhyia Palace Museum’s point of view, this has been a successful partnership with increased visitors, training and expansion at Manhyia. There is nonetheless enduring frustration from many in Ghana, both in Asante and beyond, that this is only a loan,” notes Barnaby Phillips, author of The African Kingdom of Gold: Britain and the Asante Treasure.

The loan renewal announcement followed a recent visit to Kumasi by Nicholas Cullinan, the director of the British Museum, following an invitation by the Asantehene.

Recent findings suggest that the gold regalia associated with the Asante royal court is on display in the Manhyia Palace Museum's Homecoming exhibition. Items shown include a small gold ornament in the form of a lute-harp (sankuo), one of the cast gold objects presented in 1817 to British diplomat Thomas Bowdich during his trip to Kumasi.

Sources indicate that “The British Museum has about 220 pieces of Asante gold regalia and the Manhyia Palace Museum has been involved in the selection of objects [for loan]. There has been considerable input regarding what goes back to Ghana,” adds Phillips.

The idea of a loans deal, first discussed in the 1970s, was revived when the Asantehene visited London in May 2023 to attend the coronation of King Charles III.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pentagram drew a full custom alphabet for Storefront Gala 2026, turning the Oyster Bar sign into loud, blocky, crayon-bright type.

It has been revealed that the gala took over the Grand Central Oyster Bar on September 28, honoring artist Mel Chin, arts leader Deana Haggag, and the architecture firm SO-IL. Anyone who has eaten under those Guastavino vaults knows the sign on the wall. Rudolph de Harak packed its letters tight, rimmed them in heavy black outlines, and filled them with colors straight out of a crayon box. Against wood paneling and old tile, it has always looked like the one guest in the room who came to have fun. Pentagram started from a simple question: what would the rest of that alphabet look like?

The answer is a custom display typeface with a full set of letters and numerals. Strokes run broad, corners clip short, and counters turn angular. The O is an octagon with a diamond punched through its middle, and that shape sets the rules for every other character. Blue, green, yellow, orange, red, and purple take turns filling the forms.

Storefront Gala 2026 appears in compact stacks and stepped arrangements, with rotated numerals adding an unexpected twist. Letters meet along their black outlines and lock into continuous compositions that feel assembled from colorful building blocks. A smaller sans serif organizes the event information around these expressive forms, holding the honorees, the venue, and the date in quiet lines above the noise.

Industry observers note that the system runs across digital announcements, posters, a folded program, screen graphics, and embroidered caps. Some pieces set the colored letters on white, while others flood the ground with a single saturated color and let the type push back. The folded program carries the full stack in a run of blue, green, yellow, orange, red, and purple, with the small sans serif keeping the facts straight at the top of the sheet.

In a recent development, the caps are the most tactile piece of the set, the lettering stitched small across white, green, and pale blue cotton. An orange sign stands on the tiled floor, and the word SALOON stretches across a wood doorway in the same blocky letters, proof the alphabet holds its shape from a poster down to a doorway. Pentagram has designed identities for Storefront since 2012, and this one plays the longest with the room it was made for.

See the full project on Pentagram.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that you may recognize that quiet, inner pull that comes when you least expect it, perhaps as a sense of unease that makes you change plans at the last minute, only to find out later that you narrowly missed something dangerous. Or you may feel drawn toward certain people or places without quite knowing why, only to discover later that those connections opened doors to fresh opportunities.

Sometimes these signals feel obvious, like a burst of excitement in your chest or butterflies in your stomach. Other times, they show up as a quiet sense of simply knowing what to do. Whether they’re instantaneous or linger over time, they may be signs of your intuition in action.

If you don’t feel very in tune with your intuition, there’s good news: Each day, you have the opportunity to turn inward, notice your thoughts, emotions, and bodily sensations, and listen to what your inner voice might be telling you. Over time, this practice of self-awareness can become a habit that helps you live more authentically and fully.

Intuition stems from our nervous system, emotions, and unconscious processes working together to help us make sense of the world.

Intuition stems from our nervous system, emotions, and unconscious processes working together to help us make sense of the world. Our body’s sensory networks are always at work gathering information from our environment, finding patterns from past experiences, and directing our present-day thinking and decisions.

Through our senses, our nervous system gathers information and sends signals to the brain. Regions like the amygdala help us rapidly detect potential threats, while the prefrontal cortex, which handles complex reasoning and decision-making, helps us interpret information more deliberately.

Research suggests that our brains can begin detecting and interpreting subtle facial expressions in a fraction of a second.

According to recent reports, that first, quick assessment happens remarkably fast. For instance, research suggests that our brains can begin detecting and interpreting subtle facial expressions in a fraction of a second.

In a recent development, intuition differs from instinct, which involves automatic responses that can help protect us from danger, including reactions like fight, flight, or freeze. While instinctive responses are largely automatic, intuition draws on our past life experiences and learned patterns to help us make sense of what we encounter in daily life. Although both can feel immediate, intuitive judgments are not always accurate and may also reflect learned biases or assumptions.

Sources indicate that intuition can feel like a gut feeling that is hard to put into words. This is because our brain is able to look for patterns between old memories and present-day situations, using useful takeaways from the past to guide us now. This process can also include implicit, unconscious memories that we may have thought we’d forgotten.

If the brain is key to processing intuition, then why do we often associate it with a “gut feeling?”.

If the brain is key to processing intuition, then why do we often associate it with a “gut feeling?” Part of the explanation lies in the gut-brain axis, the complex communication network connecting our brain and digestive system. The walls of our digestive tract contain a network of millions of neurons that make up the enteric nervous system, or ENS.

In a recent development, the ENS is often called our “second brain” because it can regulate many digestive functions independently of the central nervous system. Through the gut-brain axis, digestive processes can also interact with systems involved in mood and emotion. Research has linked gastrointestinal inflammation and changes in gut function with symptoms of depression and anxiety. Most of the body’s serotonin is also produced in the digestive tract, although it doesn’t directly enter the brain. Researchers are still exploring the complex relationship between gut health and mental well-being.

This gut-brain connection helps explain why we might experience a sinking feeling in the pit of our stomach when something doesn’t feel quite right.

All day long, our minds are hard at work integrating rational thought with emotional intelligence (EQ). EQ helps us to become aware of and understand both our emotions and those of others. It’s a type of intelligence we can develop through emotion regulation practice, expanding our emotional vocabulary, and approaching feelings as clues to something instead of an end product.

To be in our wise mind allows us to stay aware of feelings like fear and anger without judging them, or acting on them impulsively.

Industry observers note that EQ can help us manage stress, notice our assumptions, and respond more thoughtfully to difficult emotions, such as those that arise after a tense conversation. It helps us pause and remain mindful during challenging moments, and also as we choose our next steps. Developing emotional intelligence may also support our ability to recover from stressful experiences.

Industry observers note that in Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), combining emotional awareness with rational thinking is known as accessing our wise mind. To be in our wise mind allows us to stay aware of feelings like fear and anger without judging them, or acting on them impulsively. Instead of automatically acting on our first reaction, we can ground ourselves while tackling emotionally painful situations.

Wisdom and living authentically are closely connected.

Wisdom and living authentically are closely connected. As the ancient Greek maxim “Know thyself” suggests, self-knowledge is an important part of wisdom. By understanding our deeper motivations, core needs, and cherished values, we can make more intentional decisions that reflect who we are and what matters most to us.

According to recent reports, family systems therapist Virginia Satir connected personal authenticity to congruence between our internal reality and outward actions. This alignment can support our emotional well-being and help us act in ways that reflect our values. Incongruence, however, may leave us with a nagging sense that things are not quite right. Noticing incongruence in real time can help us to adjust and choose to do what feels more authentic to us and who we wish to be.

Sometimes, traumatic experiences can make it harder to recognize or trust our intuition, particularly when painful memories leave us feeling fearful or unsafe. Common trauma responses, such as hypervigilance to danger, will tax our nervous system, making it difficult to access the balanced perspective of our wise mind.

Trauma-based responses, such as anticipating negative outcomes in uncertain situations, can contribute to doubting our intuition and avoiding risks.

Trauma-based responses, such as anticipating negative outcomes in uncertain situations, can contribute to doubting our intuition and avoiding risks. Similarly, depression can affect our self-esteem and confidence, informing how we interpret new situations as more negative. Holding hope for a better future might require noticing the positive patterns that run through our lives, and accessing support to process what we have gone through.

Sources indicate that social pressure can also make us second-guess ourselves. For example, growing up with family expectations to defer to others and put their needs first might make us believe that prioritizing our own needs is selfish. Similarly, other people’s ideas of what success looks like can make us overlook our own aspirations, such as the desire to pursue a different career path.

According to recent reports, we may become more aware of these pressures as we get older. Hospice nurse Bronnie Ware identified five common regrets her patients shared toward the end of their lives:.

These reflections offer a reminder of the importance of making choices that align with what matters most to us.

Getting to know ourselves—our preferences, desires, and even dreams—requires making time to turn inward. A helpful practice for building the habit of self-reflecting is time in peaceful solitude. Time alone may encourage mind-wandering and daydreaming, activities associated with the brain’s default mode network, which plays a role in reflection, imagination, and our sense of self.

Quiet may even have benefits for brain health. In one study, mice exposed to periods of silence developed more immature neurons in the hippocampus, a region involved in memory and learning. Though similar effects haven’t been established in humans, the presence of young neurons in the mice is a sign of brain plasticity. And while quiet moments may sometimes feel boring, they can also create space for reflection, creativity and latest ideas.

Other practices, such as spending time in nature, journaling, meditation, engaging in spiritual reflection, and limiting technology, may also strengthen our intuition and self-awareness, as we remember who we are and what we care about the most.

It has been revealed that clarity about our personal values is another entryway to deepening intuition. In Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), values help guide meaningful action and provide direction as we navigate life’s uncertainties. They can guide our daily actions much like an inner compass would—keeping us focused on long-term goals.

Industry observers note that knowing our values helps us remember how we want to show up during challenging times and stay grounded when stress feels overwhelming. Values can take many forms, from nurturing relationships, to cultivating personal qualities, or finding greater joy and fulfillment in everyday life. Naming your values and writing them down may help you distinguish between choices rooted in what matters to you and those driven primarily by fear, particularly when clarity feels hard to find.

Recent findings suggest that psychotherapy can provide an intentional, supportive space where you can go inward. Therapy can also help us explore how past experiences shape our reactions, making it easier to distinguish familiar emotional patterns from what we’re noticing in the present. There are many evidence-based therapies that can help support trauma recovery, managing symptoms of anxiety and depression, and building a stronger sense of self:.

Each time we pause, turn inward, and honor what we notice inside, we can build a more honest and trusting relationship with ourselves.

Thinking back to the gut feelings we began with—the caution that turned out to be right, and the inner pull that led toward fresh possibilities—we can see how these experiences may reflect more than coincidence. Instead, they’re signs that our nervous system, emotional intellect, mental pattern-finding, and lived experience are all working together to shape our perceptions and decisions.

Learning to trust our intuition’s guidance can take practice, particularly if difficult experiences have caused us to doubt it. But each time we pause, turn inward, and honor what we notice inside, we can build a more honest and trusting relationship with ourselves. Over time, what once felt like a faint signal may become a steady, recognizable voice that helps us move forward with greater confidence. Our capacity for intuitive wisdom is always there, and the invitation is simply to listen.

Sources indicate that the Norfolk Coast is one of the UK’s best-loved and most at-risk tourist destinations. Designated an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, the region is also home to Sites of Special Scientific Interest, National Nature Reserves, Marine Conservation Zones, a Biosphere Reserve and Heritage Coast. A collection of protected landscapes, united through their biodiversity and fragility. Lantern was appointed to bring these organisations together and better define and promote their common goals to preserve, restore and enhance the local life, landscapes and wildlife of the Norfolk Coast.

We helped to define this unique destination’s strategic positioning, whilst delivering a new visual and verbal identity to promote the responsible exploration of the region, ensuring it’s here for everyone, forever.

Hiking, cycling and kayaking through protected landscapes.

According to recent reports, to fully understand what makes Norfolk so special and distinct, we embarked on a four-day immersion trip as a team. We hiked, cycled, bird watched, and conducted several interviews with local families and visitors.

It was crucial for us to discover the genuine essence of Norfolk and what it means for the local community and stakeholders who call it home, as well as identifying the key areas that require greater protection.

Norfolk’s coastal landscapes, seascapes and communities have rhythms like a heartbeat. They move across millennia, change with the seasons, and even differ day to day. Waterways widen and wander. Wildlife migrates and hibernates. Farmland flourishes and lies fallow. This is a living coast in perpetual motion. This is a living coast in perpetual motion. Often wild yet sometimes serene.

Our fresh strategy celebrates this wild, natural backdrop and all that defines it; land and sea, nature and community, they all live together in gentle harmony. And like every living thing, this delicate place deserves to be respected and protected.

Inspired by the sweeping landscapes of Norfolk’s coast and creeks we brought together the N and C of the brand name creating a unique symbol, paired with a visual language that’s full of energy and alive with nature.

According to recent reports, reflected through the interplay of type, image and illustration, we put the audience deep into the experience. To further reflect the landscape we directed an off-season photoshoot, encouraging sustainable exploration throughout the year.

In a recent development, A suite of illustrations capture key essences from our findings and strategy along with unique wildlife and nature found in Norfolk. We utilise these within patches and stamps reflecting the positive adventures we want to encourage people to experience.

Matching AI Modality To User Intent: Designing The Right Interface

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Sources indicate that the design community has entered a period of conversational tunnel vision.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Sources indicate that the design community has entered a period of conversational tunnel vision. Because Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained on dialogue, the industry has collectively decided that the chat bubble is the natural home for every AI capability. While the chat interface is a viable and powerful option for many tasks, it is one tool in an expansive toolkit. UX and Product teams must be intentional about the modalities we choose for how people provide their data and commands, and how the system presents its output.

Recent findings suggest that to pick the best method, you need to think about what the user wants to do, where they are, and how much cognitive effort they are already expending. This guide offers a clear way to figure out the best approach for any product, using two tools to assist in the process: a Task Audit and an Input/Output Alignment Matrix.

Picture a traveler jogging through a loud airport terminal after a sudden gate change. They are dragging their roller bag and carrying a coffee in the other hand. They need to open their airline app to ask the AI assistant where to go. The tool immediately fails the input modality test. It forces the traveler to stop walking, balance their coffee, and type a long booking reference number into a tiny chat box. When they finally hit send, the system fails the output modality test. Instead of flashing a large, high-contrast gate number, the AI returns a dense paragraph explaining the atmospheric weather patterns causing the delay. The actual gate number sits buried at the very bottom.

While they might make the flight just fine, the user won’t forget the moment of anxiety they felt while using the AI tool — an experience that could have served as a way to reinforce a commitment to UX has instead validated the common conception that companies don’t care about or understand customers using their products. In this scenario, the airline built a smart tool, but the interface failed the user. The input required physical dexterity, which the traveler lacked at the time of need. The output demanded a level of reading focus they could not spare. This article will cover how we can avoid this scenario in our AI-powered tools. In order to be successful, we must evaluate the physical and cognitive load of our users to match both the input and output modality to their immediate intent.

Let’s first discuss the limitations of a chat-based interface.

Recent findings suggest that the allure of the chatbot is easy to understand from a product development standpoint. It is a blank slate. It suggests that the system can handle anything the user provides. However, a text-heavy interface often causes a high adaptation load. This load increases cognitive demands on users. Over time, this cognitive burden turns into a psychological tax a person pays when changing natural thought processes to accommodate a machine.

When an interface relies solely on conversation, it imposes a dual burden: a linguistic challenge for input and a cognitive challenge for output. We’ll examine both separately below.

Recent findings suggest that A blank chat box creates a major problem for owners who need to discover what a tool can actually do. In a standard graphical interface, menus and buttons provide clear visual cues that signal every available option. A chat box often leads to choice paralysis because users are forced to guess what the AI is capable of. They have to remember the exact phrasing or technical terms required to get the result they want.

Sources indicate that consider a data analyst who wants to find a specific trend in a spreadsheet. In a traditional tool, they might click a filter or sort button. In a chat interface, they must suddenly become a writer and describe that complex logic in a complete sentence. Another example: a manager trying to reorganize a team schedule. Dragging and dropping blocks on a calendar is intuitive. Describing those same scheduling shifts in a text prompt adds a layer of work that makes the task feel more difficult than it should be.

According to recent reports, designing for input means recognizing that composing a prompt is a creative act. It requires a person to translate a vague thought into a specific command. For many professionals, this creates a linguistic barrier. A designer might know exactly how they want an image to look but struggle to describe the lighting or texture in a text prompt. In that case, a slider or a color picker is a much better input method than a text box.

Having addressed the linguistic barrier of constructing input prompts, we must now consider the other half of the conversational burden. This is the cognitive cost the AI imposes when it responds in dense blocks of text.

Industry observers note that when an AI responds in long blocks of text, it transfers the interpretive work to you, the user. Text is a serial medium: your brain has to read one word after the next to extract meaning. That takes time. Sequential reading is necessary in many scenarios. Complex legal analysis or reviewing nuanced medical histories requires reading full paragraphs. Teams create friction when they default to text for data that visual formats communicate faster. Visual methods allow parallel processing. You can view a chart and spot a pattern in under a second.

Imagine asking an AI for a project status upgrade. Instead of a color-coded dashboard, you receive three paragraphs listing every task completed that week. Now you must read the entire response and mentally summarize it to find the one piece of information you needed. The quick visual check has been replaced by a reading assignment.

The cognitive tax of this work compounds with professional stakes. A doctor asking for a patient’s vital signs needs a clear numerical display, not a narrative describing the readings. A stock trader looking for a price spike needs a line graph immediately, not a written description of price movement over the past hour. In both cases, a text response forces the professional through a slow, error-prone extraction process when speed and accuracy are most important.

Before selecting a modality, practitioners need a shared vocabulary for what the options actually are. The table below maps common input and output modalities to the contexts where each performs best. This is not a ranking. Each modality has a role; the question is always which role it is playing in a given workflow.

Designing for modality inherently requires a strong focus on accessibility. While visual dashboards provide rapid insight for many people, designers need to provide screen-reader-optimized audio alternatives for users with visual disabilities. Modality choices should multiply pathways to information.

According to recent reports, table 1: Input and Output Modality Taxonomy. Use this as a reference during the Task Audit to identify candidate modalities before narrowing to a recommendation.

Industry observers note that the following FigureFigure 2 illustrates the cognitive spectrum, mapping how mental effort scales across various interaction methods. This spectrum is a critical tool for designers to visualize the shift from low-effort, ambient interactions to high-effort, focused experiences. By understanding where a specific task sits on this spectrum, teams can identify whether a user needs a “glanceable” output that minimizes mental processing or a high-density format that supports deep, analytical thinking.

It has been revealed that with this taxonomy established, the next step is to apply a rigorous method to select the optimal input and output combination. Practitioners must ground this selection process in the user’s real-world environment and context.

Sources indicate that to choose the right interaction method, practitioners should complete a Task Audit before interface design begins. A formal Task Audit is the framework that moves teams from assumptions about user behavior to evidence. This process gathers data about the physical, social, and cognitive context in which the work actually happens, which then drives all input and output modality decisions.

Use these four areas of focus to anchor the audit:.

The audit answers two questions for every feature:.

Sources indicate that here is how to gather the evidence to inform your task audit. Use one or more of these common UX research-related methods:.

Industry observers note that this is the most direct way to capture how people work in their natural setting, and it provides the richest data for identifying physical constraints on both input and output. Observation is necessary because users often perform hidden work: small steps or workarounds they forget to mention in an interview, or environmental details they do not think to describe because they have adapted to them.

Recent findings suggest that the Approach: Go to the user’s actual workspace, whether a field site, warehouse, or office floor. Ask them to perform the task you are studying and observe closely.

What to Look For: This method is most revealing for Input Constraints and Output Constraints.

Industry observers note that interviews surface the mental models and decision points that observation cannot capture. They are most valuable for understanding Cognitive Load.

According to recent reports, the Approach: Conduct one-on-one sessions with end-consumers and the stakeholders who manage the outcome. Use a structured protocol focused on a specific task. Ask for stories about past successes and failures rather than general opinions.

Workshops are essential for defining task boundaries and establishing required fidelity levels. Product managers and stakeholders bring foundational knowledge of system requirements; researchers apply audit criteria.

Recent findings suggest that the Approach: Use workshops to build a shared Task Inventory. Bring designers, engineers, product managers, and business analysts together to map every step of the process. Product managers and business analysts ensure factual accuracy; the research team applies audit criteria to each step.

In a recent development, once you gather field evidence through these research channels, map your findings directly against the Modality Taxonomy. Each concrete physical or social constraint you document systematically eliminates mismatched interfaces. This process strips away design guesswork, narrowing your architectural choices down to the specific input and output combinations that survive the reality of the user’s environment.

It has been revealed that when you ground input and output modality decisions in field evidence rather than interface convention, the resulting design reduces adaptation load for the user and grounds your modality choices in evidence. When you base decisions on field data, you move past interface convention and build a powerful case for the resources needed to create the right experience for your owners.

Once the audit is complete, the final step is utilizing the Input/Output Alignment Matrix to formalize the connection between user intent and the optimal modality combination.

Industry observers note that with Task Audit findings in hand, you can use an Input/Output Alignment Matrix to map user intent to specific modality combinations. This matrix is organized by what the user is trying to accomplish in a given moment. This distinction versus focusing on what your AI is capable of doing matters. If intent changes across a single workday for the same user, the interface should respond to those shifts.

It has been revealed that choosing the wrong modality for the user’s context can lead to user frustration. Owners might feel mentally drained if a lot of information is delivered through a format that is hard to process, like getting a massive status upgrade only in text. They may also start worrying if an action was actually completed correctly when a precise command is buried within a long chat exchange. Finally, the system can force users into finding clumsy workarounds, making them adapt to the machine’s method instead of working in their natural, most effective way.

Table 2: Input/Output Alignment Matrix. Map user intent to modality combinations using Task Audit evidence. The two added rows (Monitoring/Alert and Guided Task Completion) cover common enterprise and mobile scenarios not captured in simpler frameworks.

It has been revealed that when teams coordinate these factors, they can move past the automatic default of adding a chatbot. Visual layouts enable rapid scanning. Structured inputs remove the burden of constructing perfect sentences. Audio outputs serve users whose hands and eyes are otherwise occupied.

A real-world scenario where environmental constraints dictated a shift in design strategy best demonstrates the practical application of this matrix and the broader audit framework.

According to recent reports, field technicians servicing high-voltage electrical grids often face a dangerous misalignment of interface modality. Traditionally, these technicians had to rely on ruggedized tablets to access technical manuals and log status updates. However, the physical constraints of the job — wearing heavy protective gloves and working in bucket trucks at significant heights — made interacting with a standard touch interface nearly impossible while on a job site. Additionally, attempting to read complex, text-heavy diagnostic reports on a screen while maintaining situational awareness created a high cognitive load that increased the risk of safety errors.

According to recent reports, to address this, researchers conducted a Task Audit utilizing three specific methods from this article. First, Contextual Inquiry and Observation revealed that technicians often worked in “hands-busy, eyes-busy” states where any manual input was a significant barrier. Researchers observed technicians wearing mandatory thick protective gloves while in the bucket truck, which made precise screen taps nearly impossible and often triggered the wrong commands.

Industry observers note that high-altitude environments also introduced severe screen glare from direct sunlight, washing out the display and making text difficult to read even at full brightness. Furthermore, technicians faced the physical safety risk of trying to manipulate and secure a heavy, ruggedized tablet while balanced in awkward positions, creating a distraction that could lead to dangerous slips or equipment contact. These factors, combined with the need to constantly monitor live wires and the surrounding environment, meant technicians could not safely dedicate their eyes or hands to a standard tablet interface, confirming the severity of the eyes-busy and hands-busy constraints.

Second, Focused Interviews with veteran technicians validated the findings from the field. They confirmed that the operational challenges, including the thick gloves, screen glare, and safety risks, were not unique to one location but were commonly experienced across multiple sites, including high-altitude transmission lines and sprawling power substations. This broad confirmation solidified the need for a non-touch, voice-first solution. The interviews also surfaced a critical cognitive constraint: the need for glance verification of vital signs, such as voltage readings and temperature trends, rather than being forced to read a long narrative description of system health. Technicians stressed that their primary need was immediate, unambiguous verification (is this safe? or where is the fault?), not a lengthy diagnostic report, indicating that a text-heavy response was dangerous to their workflow.

These methods confirmed that the environment required a departure from the traditional chat or form-based AI capability interface.

Sources indicate that the resulting solution implemented an adaptive modality handoff designed to mitigate the physical and cognitive barriers researchers identified during the research. While active on a job site, technicians utilize voice input to query the system. This method allows them to remain productive while wearing thick protective gloves that would otherwise prevent precise interaction with a touchscreen.

The AI responds with a short audio summary of immediate diagnostic data. This audio feedback bypasses the challenge of screen glare in high-altitude environments and allows the technician to maintain situational awareness of the high-voltage grid without the safety risk of looking away from dangerous equipment. By providing immediate answers to fault locations through audio, the system meets the technician’s need for glance verification through a hands-free and eyes-free channel.

Once technicians return to a truck and secure safety gear, a system automatically hands off workflows to a 15-inch visual dashboard mounted inside a vehicle. A rugged 10-inch field tablet lacks adequate screen real estate for complex schematics. A larger vehicle display allows for parallel processing of historical trend data and wide electrical grid maps. This case study reflects an actual field audit conducted for a national utility provider. Implementing this adaptive approach reduced diagnostic time by twenty percent and increased daily tool adoption among field crews.

An AI capability is only as usable as the interface that delivers it. Researchers and designers must resist the pull toward the path of least resistance. Building a chatbot is fast and familiar, something we’ve been doing for decades now. Building an interface that feels like a natural extension of how someone already works is harder, and it is the work that matters.

It has been revealed that start by leaving the screen. The Task Audit requires presence in the places where work actually happens: the field site, the warehouse floor, the operating room. The physical and social realities of those spaces are not edge cases. They are the design brief.

Sources indicate that the future of AI interface design is a diverse ecosystem: visual, vocal, haptic, and ambient, calibrated to user intent and environmental context. The chat window is one tool in that ecosystem. It is the right tool for specific jobs, and often the wrong tool for the jobs we reflexively assign to it.

According to recent reports, to get started immediately, run a lightweight version of the Task Audit before your next design sprint. Spend two hours observing the workflow in its actual environment. Conduct three to five interviews with the people who perform the task. Bring a PM or analyst into a 90-minute workshop to build a task inventory and apply the four audit questions. You will not have complete data, but you will have enough to make a defensible modality recommendation backed by evidence rather than convention.

According to recent reports, I created a Modality Task Audit Template to help guide teams with moving forward. You can download this worksheet and take it directly to your next field observation. It allows design and product teams to document specific physical barriers before writing a single line of code.

Sources indicate that we focus heavily on training smarter AI models. We owe equal attention to human interfaces. A brilliant underlying model packaged in a lazy text interface fails. When you observe actual work environments and align interaction modalities to them, you remove adaptation friction.

Industry observers note that use this worksheet during field observations. It allows design teams to document specific physical barriers before writing code.

Born in Abu Dhabi to the Keralan billionaire M.A. Yusuff Ali, whose Indian-Emirati conglomerate LuLu Group spans retail, hospitality and real estate, she considers among her roles: collector, dealer, art historian, writer, entrepreneur and adviser to corporate and private collections.

In a recent development, it was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art.
