Building A UX ROI Case That Survives The Boardroom

📅 2026-09-11 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2579 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alex Williams is a seasoned full-stack developer and the former owner of Hosting Data UK.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Sources indicate that sooner or later, a CFO looks at your wireframes and asks what any of it actually does for the bottom line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alex Williams is a seasoned full-stack developer and the former owner of Hosting Data UK. After graduating from the University of London with a Masters Degree … More about Alex ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Sources indicate that sooner or later, a CFO looks at your wireframes and asks what any of it actually does for the bottom line. Storyboards don’t answer that question, and the era when a 5-minute pitch could answer it ended, unfortunately, a while ago.

These days, if you want to win budget, buy-in, and backing for UX, the design has to be provably good for the business, not only for the people using it.

Sources indicate that and proving that takes more than taping a dollar sign to a redesign. You have to understand how your organization defines value in the first place, how it measures that value, and how a credible line gets drawn between a design initiative and an outcome leadership already cares about.

Recent findings suggest that rather than scatter tips, this article follows one worked example the whole way through. Meridian is a mid-size B2B SaaS organization, and it is entirely made up — that label matters, so it gets repeated where it counts. Its onboarding redesign carries the same figures from goal-setting through cost accounting, causal testing, and the final ROI number, because a framework only becomes tangible when the numbers connect. Every step is one you can rerun inside your own organization.

In a recent development, companies now want clarity on what every dollar buys, and “delightful user experiences” stopped clearing that bar some time ago. I still remember a former colleague celebrating a $1 million redesign he’d gotten greenlit mostly on the strength of a couple of three.js tricks. Try that pitch in front of a finance team today and see how far the particles get you.

Executives don’t hate UX, they just hate vagueness. A pitch built on “people will find it easier” loses, every time, to the department promising 12% more sales in Q3. The difference is the one between a streamlined checkout flow that reduced cart abandonment with completed purchases up 22%, and the same work rewarded with “the QA testers like it.” One of those goes on your resume. The rest of this article is about earning the first version, with Meridian’s numbers doing the work.

It has been revealed that most writing about UX ROI makes a convenient assumption: that the organization already owns clean business goals and KPIs for you to hook your work onto. Real companies are messier than that. Plenty run on ambitions like “grow faster” or “improve the customer journey” that nobody ever broke into anything measurable, and an ROI case built on that ambiguity sounds impressive right up until somebody scrutinizes it.

So the first job is often to help the organization define what success even looks like. Interview stakeholders across departments — what does product consider a good quarter, where does customer success watch consumers struggle, where do sales deals stall — and listen for the themes that keep resurfacing across conversations, because those recurring themes are the firm’s latent business objectives. A useful forcing function is the OKR model (Objectives and Key Results), which doesn’t tolerate vagueness.

In a recent development, at Meridian, the stated ambition was “improve the rate of new customers’ adoption of the platform,” which you can neither design toward nor measure against. Interviews turned up the real shape of the problem. Trial users needed a median of 14 days to reach first value, most churned before getting there, and onboarding questions were burying the support queue. Out of that came an OKR with actual edges: reduce median time-to-first-value from 14 days to 7 with the use of a guided setup flow, and lift trial-to-paid conversion from 8% to 9.5%.

Recent findings suggest that one warning about formalizing KPIs: Impose them from inside the UX team and leadership will suspect you’ve rigged the field in your own favor, so co-create them with whoever owns the outcome — though never at the price of accepting targets that set your team up for an uncomfortable situation. Meridian’s head of product agreed that setup-completion rate was a fair proxy for onboarding usability, and customer success signed off on time-to-first-value, a number already sitting on their own dashboard.

ROI has a denominator, and the denominator is where most UX teams go wrong. You can’t calculate a return without strategic financial planning, yet cost usually gets counted as designer salaries or consulting hours and nothing else. A finance team will find the rest whether or not you counted it, so count it first.

According to recent reports, direct costs are the visible ones. Meridian’s redesign ran $45,000 in design and research labor plus another $8,000 in tooling and participant incentives. Licenses for Figma, UserTesting, Hotjar, analytics platforms, research incentive spend — all of it belongs in the total, and that’s before the inevitable instances of vendor lock-in every UX team eventually faces. Engineering sits in the same column, because a UX redesign doesn’t stop at the mockup. Building the guided setup took two frontend sprints plus a QA pass, $38,000 worth, and the project generated about $4,000 of coordination overhead along the way in fresh syncs and shared dashboards.

Sources indicate that the line item nearly everyone misses, and the one worth stealing from this article if you steal nothing else, is stakeholder time. Workshops, design reviews, and feedback sessions all pull senior people away from their primary work. A VP of Product spending four hours a week in UX reviews is a VP not spending those hours on roadmap planning or partner negotiations. Log the attendance — who came, for how long, at what seniority — and price it at fully loaded cost, meaning salary plus benefits divided by productive hours. A quarter’s worth of workshops, reviews, and interviews at Meridian priced out at $22,000.

Add it all up: $45,000 in design labor, $8,000 in tooling, $38,000 in engineering, $22,000 in stakeholder time, $4,000 in coordination. The investment is $117,000. Saying that number out loud beats saying “we spent $45K on design,” precisely because it already includes everything a finance team would have dug up on its own.

Most UX ROI pitches die right here. Conversions rose after the redesign, sure — and the CFO wants to know how you ruled out the newly introduced pricing, the seasonal traffic bump, and the marketing campaign that shipped the same week. Without a convincing answer, your entire ROI story crumbles.

After all these years, the gold standard for proving causation is still A/B testing: run the old experience against the upcoming one on an even traffic split until the sample means something.

Recent findings suggest that onboarding happens to suit a phased rollout, which is why Meridian could do this cleanly. For eight weeks, half of new trial signups received the redesigned guided setup while half stayed on the legacy flow. Control converted to paid at 8.0%. The variant came in at 9.4%. With roughly 6,100 trials inside the window, the difference was statistically significant, but a 1.4-point gap on a single test is still the kind of result that deserves a second look before anyone builds a budget on it, which is one reason the team held back on attribution below. Where a split isn’t feasible — a change too structural, a user base too small — fall back to a time series instead. Measure steadily for weeks before the change, implement, then keep measuring against the baseline you established.

Documenting whatever else happens around the same time as your UX change is the unglamorous half of causation.

According to recent reports, A pricing-page test from Meridian’s marketing team overlapped weeks five through eight of the rollout. The UX team noted it, confirmed it hit both cohorts evenly, and still chose to attribute only 70% of the observed lift to the redesign in the final math. There is no formula that produces that number; treat it as an illustrative assumption for this example.

Sources indicate that the team asked how much of the lift could plausibly belong to the pricing test if it had helped one cohort slightly more than the other, settled on a ceiling of about a third, and rounded the redesign’s share down to 70%. Your figure will differ. What matters is that it is written down and argued for before the results arrive, not fitted to them afterwards. That restraint is worth money in a skeptical room. “We attribute roughly 70% of the lift to the onboarding change, with the remainder likely influenced by concurrent pricing work” survives cross-examination; claiming everything does not. Cohort analysis then backed the number up, since the lift held across acquisition channels and tenure bands, and at that point the skeptics had very little left to work with.

Recent findings suggest that leading and lagging indicators belong on the same slide, because each covers the other’s weakness. Meridian’s leading indicators moved first — setup completion climbed from 62% to 89%, median time-to-first-value dropped from 14 days to 6.5 — and the lagging trial-to-paid number followed. Mechanism first, business outcome second. Presented together, they form a causal chain that’s harder to poke holes in than either one alone.

So what did Meridian actually earn? The organization sees about 40,000 trial signups a year. Lifting conversion from 8.0% to 9.4% adds roughly 560 paying customers annually, and at an average of $1,800 in annual recurring revenue per account, those customers represent about $1,008,000 in new ARR. Applying the conservative 70% attribution from the causal work trims the defensible figure to roughly $706,000.

Set that against the full $117,000 investment and the first-year ROI lands near 5:1, with payback arriving in roughly two months. There’s a second line, too. Onboarding-related support tickets dropped about 30%, some 3,600 fewer tickets a year, worth another $54,000 annually at $15 per resolved ticket. Keep it as its own line rather than folding it into one swollen headline number. The case reads as more honest that way and loses none of its force.

Recent findings suggest that three assumptions carry that result, and each belongs on the slide next to it. The 40,000 signups and the $1,800 average ARR are the prior year’s actuals held flat, so a growth or pricing change moves the outcome in either direction. The 70% attribution is the illustrative assumption from the causal work, not a measured quantity. And the two-month payback counts upcoming ARR as it lands rather than revenue recognized net of churn, which flatters the timeline; on a net basis the payback stretches to roughly a quarter. State those three plainly and a finance team can adapt the example to its own numbers. Hide them and the whole thing starts to look like marketing math, however careful the experiment was.

What persuades in the final presentation is not sophistication. Open with the baseline: what stalled trials and support volume were already costing. Show the delta in terms leadership reads fluently, metrics like conversion rate uplift chief among them. A chart of setup completion climbing from 62% to 89% will beat a paragraph of UX jargon, and a translation like “each abandoned setup costs us 0.3 support tickets” beats the chart. Above all, keep every figure identical from the first slide to the last. A room full of finance people forgives many things, but never numbers that wobble between slides.

Recent findings suggest that budget decisions come out of coalitions. A CFO may hold the final say when adding AI to the checkout process, but marketing, product, and customer success all lean on that decision, and each means something different by “value.”.

A CFO hears cost, revenue, and risk. A CMO hears conversion and acquisition cost, since UX is a lever for increasing marketing ROI. Product counts support tickets; customer success thinks in retention. The underlying numbers never change; only the framing rotates, and a CFO wants a projection, not a moodboard. Meridian’s CFO slide read “the onboarding redesign protects roughly $706,000 in new ARR a year against a $117,000 investment,” while the CMO version led with what a 9.4% trial conversion does to blended acquisition cost.

Some UX outcomes never translate cleanly into revenue, and pretending they do weakens the parts of your case that are solid.

Scores like Net Promoter Score (NPS), CSAT, and Customer Effort Score already sit inside most reporting cadences, which makes them cheap to borrow. Tie your work to their movement, and segment wherever the data allows.

According to recent reports, meridian could say that NPS among trial users on the redesigned onboarding was 51 against 34 for the legacy flow, which lands far harder than any blended average. Verbatim feedback from surveys, support transcripts, and app store reviews adds the emotional weight the scores lack. Internal tools deserve the same discipline, since employee experience is increasingly recognized as a business driver — a dashboard redesign that hands account managers 45 minutes a day back is a productivity gain, a satisfaction gain, and a retention lever all in one.

Sources indicate that brand perception resists direct measurement but leaves tracks in repeat visits, organic referrals, and social sentiment. It carries extra weight in trust-sensitive industries like finance or healthcare, and it forms fast, given that UX design influences the first impressions of a whopping 94% of customers.

Whatever you collect, systematize the collecting. Run pre- and post-surveys with consistent question sets, use structured usability testing with task-based scoring, and put the qualitative right next to the quantitative when you present.

UX loses the budget battle unless it’s mapped to company-wide objectives, so phrase the proposal in the words of this year’s board presentation.

It has been revealed that nobody at Meridian pitched “simplify the onboarding UI”; the pitch was a redesigned trial experience worth 1.4 points of upgrade rate, roughly $1M in annual recurring revenue before attribution. Bring evidence in both registers, since that is what social proof is for: the case, clearly labeled, plus screenshots, impact graphs, and user quotes. Find internal allies who can repeat the ROI narrative in rooms you’ll never enter, and write the playbook down, because repeatable ROI is what earns recurring investment.

This topic has been explored extensively by researchers, practitioners, and consultancies. Here’s a curated set of resources worth studying if you want to build a stronger ROI practice around UX.

A seat at the table never comes from beauty or novelty. It comes from measurable, defensible impact, which means UX leaders have to trade the artist’s posture for the strategist’s. Speak in outcomes rather than outputs. Connect pixels to profit.

When someone challenges the numbers, don’t flinch. Show the controlled experiment, the cohort analysis, and the before-and-after metrics, every figure holding steady from the first slide to the last, the way Meridian’s did, with the customer quotes and the employee-satisfaction data sitting right beside the revenue impact. Prove the work does more than delight users, and be ready to defend the ratio line by line. That’s when the CFO leans in, and that’s when design stops being optional.

How Klafs Is Rethinking the Sauna Through Design

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the sauna is Finnish.
  • Recent findings suggest that at Klafs headquarters, where the tech giant’s newest ideas are developed and tested, the tour begins in a two-tiered, glass-enclosed sauna.
  • In German, aufguss means “infusion,” or literally “pouring over.” In a wellness context, it refers to a guided sauna ritual, typically involving water poured over hot stones, aromatic infusions, and the circulation of heated air.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the sauna is Finnish. The manufacturer reimagining it for contemporary homes and spas is German. Klafs, based in Schwäbisch Hall, Germany, sees no contradiction. Its designers approach the centuries-old ritual through engineering, experimenting with heat, air, and materials. As wellness culture expands, the language surrounding its rituals has become increasingly fluid. In my own friend group, “banya” has become nearly shorthand for any spa visit, though it refers specifically to the Russian-style bathhouse. Klafs, by contrast, brings a distinctly German engineering sensibility to these traditions, asking how far the experience can be pushed.

Recent findings suggest that at Klafs headquarters, where the tech giant’s newest ideas are developed and tested, the tour begins in a two-tiered, glass-enclosed sauna. Our guide, an experienced training manager named Heinrich, speaks to the heater in the corner. “Hey, Klafs,” he indicates, with the intonation we’ve learned from Alexa and other voice-activated devices. I hadn’t considered the possibility of a smart aufguss guide.

In German, aufguss means “infusion,” or literally “pouring over.” In a wellness context, it refers to a guided sauna ritual, typically involving water poured over hot stones, aromatic infusions, and the circulation of heated air. The practice has helped make sauna-going a communal experience in many North American spas. Klafs’s Vitality Boost, which the firm describes as the world’s first personalized heat-waving system, brings elements of that ritual into an automated setting: no towel-spinning guide required, and no need to leave the wooden bench.

Blue lighting, textured surfaces, and a sculptural ice fountain transform Klafs’s Frimas ice steam room into an immersive cooling environment. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

In a recent development, from the heat of the sauna, the tour moves into an altogether different climate. I retreat into the cool blue light of a Frimas ice steam room, where a glowing central ice fountain grows delicate, flower-like formations.

Recent findings suggest that around the corner, a button labeled “snow” summons flurries from the ceiling of the ice steam shower. The cooling phase of a hot-and-cold bathing ritual isn’t where most people want to linger, but these spaces make a compelling case for slowing down. Rather than treating cold exposure as something to endure, KLAFS creates immersive environments that make it part of the experience.

Klafs brings the experience of winter indoors with a snow room featuring ice-covered surfaces, dramatic lighting, and a rocky landscape. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

In a recent development, then there’s the foam. I also discovered foam steam baths, which replace the intensity of a traditional aufguss with a more playful, tactile experience. Steam rooms equipped for foam treatments can be integrated into hotel and spa programming as scheduled group experiences. The suds, reminiscent of childhood bubble baths and the elaborate foam sculptures they inspired, bring out a part of my inner child I had long since stowed away. Espuro, Klafs’s proprietary foam essence, is formulated with plant-based ingredients, including coconut-derived compounds, which the company says help care for skin exposed to heat.

Industry observers note that designed in collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, Klafs’s S11 sauna incorporates horizontal wood slats and integrated lighting into a contemporary residential interior. Photographycourtesy of Klafs.

Beyond these sensory experiments, Klafs has also reconsidered the sauna itself as an architectural object. The retractable S1 sauna expands from a compact enclosure into a full-size sauna, addressing the spatial constraints that often keep one out of the home. The design-led S11, a collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, pairs delicate washi paper and multicolor light panels with smooth, sinuous lines.

Inside the S11, continuous horizontal slats, curved corners, and concealed lighting create a sculptural interior that emphasizes materiality and form. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Recent findings suggest that long established in Germany, Klafs has been expanding into the American market since its acquisition by Kohler in 2024. The premium Altea fitness club in my city, for instance, features Klafs installations, including the Sanarium and Polaris Ice Room. Yet what stays with me after the visit isn’t a particular product. It’s the willingness to question what a sauna, steam room, or cooling space can be. At Klafs, even the most familiar wellness rituals seem open to reinvention.

Warm wood surfaces, tiered seating, and integrated lighting define a Klafs sauna at Hotel Sonne-Post, a spa hotel in Waldau, Germany. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Bianca Weeko Martin is a writer and researcher whose work explores the intersection of architectural practice, theory, and personal narrative. She is the author of Architectural Guide Manila.

#80184. Stop Treating CSS Container Queries Like Traditional Media Queries

📅 2026-09-16 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2082 w)

Stop Treating CSS Container Queries Like Traditional Media Queries

📅 2026-09-16 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2082 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I Code.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • In a recent development, to be completely honest with you, I missed the news when CSS Container Queries first shipped.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I Code. I Write. Meme Rules. Ok, but seriously, I’m a web and mobile developer who writes a lot. In my spare time, I like to build products that would … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In a recent development, to be completely honest with you, I missed the news when CSS Container Queries first shipped. And when I finally heard about it, my very first thought was, “Why exactly do I need this when media queries already exist?”.

I’m not proud of that reaction, knowing what I know now, but it was comforting to know that I wasn’t alone. In fact, there are legions of us out there.

What baffles me is that container queries aren’t a upcoming feature, as it currently sits at around 94% browser support. And yet, very few people are actually using it. According to the State of CSS survey, 86% of developers are aware of container queries, but only 41.4% actually use them. Surveys can be biased and not completely representative of our entire field, but this one is certainly the best indicator we’ve got.

Sources indicate that kevin Powell also talked about this at SmashingConf Amsterdam 2026: Container Queries adoption has been terrible. And that is so strange to me, knowing that the ability for components to adapt to the size of their outer container has been at the top of so many CSS wishlists over the years.

I’m not particularly interested in how many people are using container queries as much as in how they are using them. I can’t account for everyone, but from what I’ve seen — including in my own early attempts — many of us are using them wrong.

In a recent development, the bottom line is that incorrect use comes down to the same impression I had when learning about them: they absolutely look just like media queries at first glance. And since they look similar, it’s easy to assume they serve similar purposes and work the same way.

Industry observers note that note: I should state up front that what I’m focusing on in this article is using container size queries, i.e., a responsive design technique for responding to the size of a particular container. There are also container style queries that respond to a container’s computed styles (and are experimental at the time of this writing). You can catch up on those in Juan Diego’s piece here on Smashing Magazine where he examines their possible use cases.

The viewport is a proxy. It always has been. Media queries are what gave us the illusion that screen width alone is responsible for how responsive apps adapt to their environment.

Ask yourself this: When you write @media, what are you asking the browser?

According to recent reports, I, like most developers, am asking the browser: How wide is the screen right now? That’s it.

Media queries answer that beautifully, but what happens when this .card component is placed in a grid cell that’s 300px wide on a 1920px desktop screen?

In a recent development, the media query doesn’t care; it does its job. The viewport is still 1920px, so min-width: 1024px fires and the matched query styles are applied, even though the card only has 300px of space to work with. Eventually, everything in the card deforms, overflows, or cramps up.

It’s common to think of responsive design purely as a system for updating complete page layouts, like going from two columns on a large screen to a single column on a small screen.

Industry observers note that container queries are smarter than that. They make responsive layouts more reliant on what’s happening inside a component rather than on the outer context that has no insight into a component’s contents. It is more like: “How much space is available for me in this specific spot, right now?”.

Here is the same card code example we looked at in the last section, but with a container query:.

According to recent reports, this changes everything. The card isn’t influenced by the viewport; its only concern is whether the .card component’s parent wrapper has at least 450px of inline (i.e., horizontal in a left-to-right writing mode) space. If that condition is true, the component goes horizontal; if not, it goes to its default block display.

See the Pen [Viewport vs Container [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a73d-6f39-709f-8dae-037f6b588852) by Vayo.

A very interesting way to distinguish @media and @container queries is the layout type.

In a recent development, media queries are for the “macro” layout; they look outward. Stuff like page structure, the header that spans the window, footers, main grid layout, system preferences (prefers-color-scheme), device capabilities (touch screens). You know, anything that is majorly true to the entire page structure.

Container queries, I’d say, are for “micro” layouts, i.e., most things that live inside the “macro” layout. We use them when any content needs to responsively fit whatever space it is allocated. Components that come to mind are things like cards, widgets, forms, navigation, and so on.

In a recent development, in other words, think “page layout” vs. “component layout”.

Sources indicate that an element shouldn’t magically become “tablet-sized” just because the width exceeds an abstract width threshold like 768px. Instead, it should switch layout when it has enough space to do so, whether that happens on a mobile viewport or inside a desktop sidebar.

In case you’re still not convinced, did you know there are over 2,300 unique viewport sizes on the modern web? Do you think it is possible to account for all of them?

I’m not hating on media queries. It’s that in this era of responsiveness and component re-use, layout logic is closer to the container than the viewport. When we think in terms of containers and components, we’re effectively relying on the content to determine layout, not the viewport.

Recent findings suggest that responsive typography is a good example of something many of us have relied on media queries for. The fact that media queries come with their own CSS units — e.g., vw, vh, and so on — that are relative to the viewport size makes media queries look really good for adjusting font size based on the user’s screen size.

This works until that same component is moved into a different context, like a sidebar, where the viewport is completely irrelevant. Now, because we tied the responsiveness to the wrong reference point, the scaled typography can get too major or too small.

Container queries come with their very own units — cqi, cqw, cqb, among others — and we can take responsive components further by coupling those units with the CSS clamp() function, using it for fluid typography that scales with the component rather than the viewport:.

See the Pen [Fluid Typography [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a73f-1a44-750c-8b40-9b0ab774d981) by Vayo.

With this in place, the entire code is self-contained to that element’s specific container.

Interestingly, container queries can, in a way, detect the state of a component’s internal layout. It’s not bulletproof, but it is also something media queries simply cannot do because they only observe the external browser window and are structurally blind to internal layout events like when, for example, flex items wrap onto a upcoming line. Let’s poke at that.

Flexbox is superb at wrapping content (flex-wrap: wrap), allowing flex items to automatically wrap to fresh lines when the flex container runs out of space to fit them in a single row. But CSS by itself can’t tell when that wrap happens. There isn’t something like a :wrapped pseudo-class or a media query like @media (flex-wrapped: true) that would get us there.

Industry observers note that media queries only observe the browser window, as they can’t see internal changes. That is pretty much what flex wrapping is: a width state change on the item itself.

For example, if you have a horizontal menu that is lined up with flexbox and you want the items to restyle themselves only when wrapped, you’d be in JavaScript territory, using ResizeObserver to get that information. However, when we nest container queries inside flex items, we can come up with a workaround to get what we need without JavaScript, thanks to this technique I learned from Kevin Powell. The core idea is to allow a flex item to flex-grow: 1 when we query the container’s inline size.

See the Pen [Fluid Typography [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a73f-1a44-750c-8b40-9b0ab774d981) by Vayo.

This works. As the parent size shrinks and the cards wrap to two lines, the card item expands, the container query fires, and applies the necessary styles.

See the Pen [Flex Wrap Detection Using Container Queries [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a752-150a-754e-a77a-07fe1b046658) by Vayo.

Container queries, like all things, come with some side effects or caveats you will want to watch for before reaching for them.

Container queries need something similar to a parent-child relationship to function as expected. Let’s say we have this markup:.

We can’t actually query the .card component to adjust the .card-content, like this:.

Industry observers note that this doesn’t work because a container cannot query itself. In that last example, we’re querying a card container and then attempting to adjust that container’s display based on its size. It’s an infinite loop.

Instead, we need an additional wrapper that makes the .card a descendant of the container:.

From there, we can query the .cards container and adjust the .card layout accordingly:.

It has been revealed that in media queries, this doesn’t matter as @media does not care which element you style inside the block; its only concern is the viewport, which is always available. So you can just slap a condition on any element and call it a day.

This happens when querying the container’s size (i.e., its block, or vertical, size) instead of its inline-size:.

Recent findings suggest that why? Because the browser calculates the container’s dimensions without looking at its children. If we don’t give the .hero-banner an explicit height (or min-height or aspect-ratio), the browser sets a height of 0px.

Sources indicate that for that reason, it’s often better to query a container by its inline-size instead. That is, unless you genuinely need to query the container’s block size.

Media queries aren’t affected by this, as they treat height the same way they treat @media (min-height: ...) does, i.e., ask the viewport and move on.

Another container query limitation: we can’t query against a custom property value:.

Sources indicate that this is because custom properties depend on values that cascade down the DOM tree. There’s the possibility that a container query that relies on a custom property can change that same custom property. And it can quickly get complicated:.

Sources indicate that I don’t think any project should wholesale use @container instead of @media. Media queries still play an notable role in responsive layouts. It’s about understanding the separation of concerns.

Sources indicate that I tend to reach for container queries when a component is used in more than one layout context. For example, a .card element could live in a full-width grid or a narrower sidebar. If that’s the case, then we’ll want the component’s content to determine when it adjusts rather than a media query that looks at the outer viewport.

Similarly, I reach for media queries when a component solely exists at the page level. This would be something like a main navigation that always sits at the top of the page. It is directly influenced by the viewport’s size, meaning that the viewport is a reliable reference for when the navigation needs to adjust. Again, it’s all about “macro” layout versus “micro” layouts.

Here’s a diagram for how I reason about which type of query to use:.

At the end of the day, the core reason why container queries look incredibly similar to media queries is simply familiarity. They’re not exactly “newly introduced”, but they are way less understood and adopted than media queries. But media queries have plenty of their own limitations; otherwise, we wouldn’t need container queries to fill those gaps.

What we have is a more effective feature for detecting when a specific component’s context changes and a means for adjusting styles based on its content, as it should be when that component can exist in multiple contexts.

Friday Five With Sarah Meyohas: Art, Science, and AI in ‘Phase Transition’

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In 2015, Meyohas debuted Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork.
  • Meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk, a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, conceptual artist and technologist Sarah Meyohas explores the intersections of art, science, and finance, translating complex systems into visual experiences. Her work examines how emerging technologies challenge our understanding of intelligence, agency, and the boundaries between living and artificial systems.

In 2015, Meyohas debuted Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork. An early experiment in blockchain-based art ownership, the project preceded Ethereum’s launch by several months.

Meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk, a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole. Her interest in this approach deepened through conversations with scientists whose research challenged familiar distinctions between the biological and the technological. “Learning about their work consistently evoked a feeling that our categories of life, computation, intelligence, and agency were becoming increasingly unstable,” she explains.

According to recent reports, ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Latest York.

It has been revealed that A Manhattan native with a B.A. in international relations from the University of Pennsylvania and a B.S. in finance from the Wharton School, Meyohas later earned an MFA from Yale. Named to Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list, she has exhibited at the Centre Pompidou in Paris, the ICA in London, and the Fresh Museum in New York. Beyond her studio practice, she invests in companies that reflect her ethical and aesthetic interests, including Sita Bio, which develops artificial womb technology.

It has been revealed that for today’s Friday Five, we spend five minutes with Sarah Meyohas to learn about the inspirations behind Phase Transition, her latest installation debuting with Marianne Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026.

According to recent reports, ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Newly introduced York.

“The title, ‘Phase Transition,’ refers to the moment matter changes state from liquid to solid,” Meyohas explains. “The sculpture holds both states simultaneously: the solid body is a form that has arrived, while the ferrofluid inside remains in motion, still becoming.”.

Industry observers note that the work began with an image that surfaced unexpectedly. “I imagined a rubber-like body with a tail tapering into a power cord plugged into the wall. I can’t point to a particular visual influence,” she notes. “It was more a continuation of a feeling, an image that seemed to arrive fully formed.”.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Latest York.

Sources indicate that that initial vision developed into a series of black, rubbery, organic forms that sprawl across mesh bases, droop down walls, and hang from suspended wires. Windows cut into several structures reveal glass tanks filled with ferrofluid, a liquid containing nanoparticles that respond to magnetic fields. Programmed magnets beneath the tanks direct the fluid into shifting patterns, while synthesizers housed in the mesh pedestals translate those movements into sound.

According to recent reports, ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Upcoming York.

What began as a singular sculpture evolved into a network of communicating bodies. “They could become a social system, with relationships, affinities, disagreements, and moments of consensus,” Meyohas states. Rather than conveying a decipherable message, the installation suggests a conversation whose emotional contours can be sensed but not understood.

That ambiguity parallels questions about a future in which artificial intelligence systems communicate increasingly among themselves, potentially in ways humans cannot interpret. “We tend to assume that intelligence will make itself legible to us, or that we will always be participants in the conversation,” Meyohas notes. “But we may find ourselves increasingly on the outside, observing exchanges between intelligences whose internal logic we can’t access.”.

In a recent development, ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Upcoming York.

Industry observers note that neuroscience research also informs the work’s atmosphere. Rather than illustrating scientific principles, Meyohas evokes the experience of observing an experiment: “the hum of equipment, the clinical posture of looking down into controlled environments, the beauty of watching something operate at a level just beyond full comprehension.”.

Here, Meyohas shares three influences that helped shape the installation, in her own words.

Photography by S. Kriegman, D. Blackiston, M. Levin, and J. Bongard; courtesy of Creative Commons.

In a recent development, “Michael Levin is a developmental biologist at Tufts University whose lab studies bioelectricity, the electrical signals cells use to coordinate where an eye or a limb should grow. His idea that problem-solving happens well below the level of the brain, in tissues and groups of cells, changed how I look at matter. His lab also helped create xenobots, tiny living machines made from frog cells that move and organize themselves.”.

Teshima Museum on Teshima Island, Japan, designed by architect Ryue Nishizawa, co-founder of SANAA, and artist Rei Naito. Photography by Epiq; courtesy of Creative Commons.

“I visited the Teshima Art Museum, by the architect Ryue Nishizawa and the artist Rei Naito, on a day when it was raining hard, and the rain fell straight through the two openings in its concrete shell. Then water began coming up through tiny holes in the floor, beading into droplets that merged and slid slowly across the concrete, pulled by gravity and the floor’s slight slope. Naito’s piece, Matrix, makes water look as if it moves by its own will.”.

A mother sperm whale and her calf off the coast of Mauritius. Photography by Gabriel Barathieu; courtesy of Creative Commons.

“Sperm whales communicate in codas, short patterns of clicks that they trade back and forth, taking turns and sometimes overlapping. In 2024, researchers with Project CETI found that codas vary in rhythm, tempo, small shifts in timing, and an occasional extra click, and that whales in an exchange match each other’s timing as they go. Combined, these features work like a phonetic alphabet, yet no one knows what the whales are saying.”.

Phase Transition (2026) will be on view with Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026, at the Miami Beach Convention Center. VIP previews take place Dec. 2–3.

According to recent reports, A 25-plus-year veteran of the interior design industry, Danine Alati began her career at commercial design publication Contract, where she spent 11 years before moving into luxury lifestyle media and working on titles including Hamptons and Art Basel. Based in Brooklyn with her family, she has contributed to AD PRO, DuJour, Galerie, and aspire, among other design and lifestyle publications.

  • Robert Manley, Phillips’ chairman and worldwide head of Modern and contemporary art, said in a statement that there had been strong bidding across Modern, post-war and contemporary art: “Nearly 90% of the works offered had never been previously sold at auction, with many of the sale’s works coming from esteemed private collections where they had been for decades.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A striking limestone head by Amedeo Modigliani sold for $44.6m (with fees) at Phillips Modern and contemporary evening sale last night (17 November), leading a nearly sold-out auction totalling $85.75m ($104.4m with fees). That is an increase of 55% from the same sale last November, which topped out at $54.8m ($67.3m with fees).

Robert Manley, Phillips’ chairman and worldwide head of Modern and contemporary art, said in a statement that there had been strong bidding across Modern, post-war and contemporary art: “Nearly 90% of the works offered had never been previously sold at auction, with many of the sale’s works coming from esteemed private collections where they had been for decades. Tonight’s results are a powerful reminder that truly exceptional works continue to inspire extraordinary competition in the market.”.

According to recent reports, sales were brisk in a bustling room, the pace in part due to the large number of works backed by third party guarantees. With just 22 lots on offer—the house withdrew Derek Fordjour’s Haberdasher, estimated at $350,000 to $550,000, at the last minute—14 carried a guarantee.

It took less than a minute and a half, for instance, for auctioneer Henry Highley to hammer Claude Monet’s La Maison dans les roses (1925) at $3.2m, matching the $4m high estimate with fees.

Claude Monet's La Maison dans les roses.

On the other hand, the Modigliani, also guaranteed, sparked a ten-minute three-way battle, escalating from the starting bid of $18m to $28m in just a few seconds before slowing to $100,000 increments. A phone bidder speaking with Phillips specialist India Phillips ultimately prevailed over clients on the line with specialists Jeremiah Evarts and Kevie Yang, placing the winning bid at $38.2m ($44.6m with fees) on an estimate of $28m to $35m.

The piece, dating from 1911 to 1912, is one of just 28 sculptures by the artist, and part of a larger series of limestone heads each titled Tête. The price, while impressive, failed to approach the $70.7m achieved by another work from the series at Sotheby’s New York in 2014, which remains the record for Modigliani sculptures. His painting record, $170.4m for the 1918 painting Nu couché—the sixth most expensive work ever to sell at auction—dates to the following year.

The evening’s second-biggest lot was David Hockney’s eight-panel oil painting David, Celia, Stephen and Ian, London 1982, which sold for $10m ($12.2m with fees) within its $10m to $15m estimate. The artist, who died in June at the age of 88, made the work in 1982. It reflects his experiments at the time with photographing a subject from slightly different, overlapping viewpoints to create Cubist-inspired collages, and marks Hockney’s return to painting after a period focused on photography.

Helen Frankenthaler's Seabreeze.

The painting, which was sold by the Joel and Carole Bernstein family collection, also boasts an impressive museum pedigree, including appearances at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, and the National Portrait Gallery in London.

It has been revealed that rounding out the sale’s top three was Alexander Calder’s 1959 mobile Snow Flurry, May 14—one of the few works without a third-party guarantee, and being sold by the family of Brazilian art critic Mário Pedrosa. Yang caused some excitement when she raised her bid straight from $4.6m to $6m, a price no one else was willing to top. The total with fees was $7.5m, above a high estimate of $6m.

Industry observers note that helen Frankenthaler had the sale’s top result for a woman artist with Seabreeze (1980), which went for $4.5m (with fees). Frankenthaler followed that up a few lots later with Peacock Alley (1990) $2.7m (with fees), right in the middle of its $2m to $3m estimate.

Recent findings suggest that the night’s only bought-in lot was Anselm Kiefer’s Melancholia (2005), which carried an estimate of $650,000 to $850,000, but bidding stalled out at just $500,000. The rust-coated painting features a polyhedral glass-and-iron sculpture mounted on the canvas.

David Hockney's David, Celia, Stephen, Ian, London August 1982 (Four Friends) (1982).

And while Jackson Pollock’s 1946 abstraction Constellation did find a buyer, the work failed to meet its low estimate of $3.5m. Despite the current show of Pollock and his wife Lee Krasner uptown at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and a provenance boasting the legendary dealer Peggy Guggenheim, the work hammered at just $2.6m ($3.3m with fees). Frank Stella’s Port Tampa City, from the estate of the late dealer Robert Mnuchin, also hammered below estimate, at $2.8m ($3.5m with fees) despite an estimate of $3m to $5m. The orange canvas, in the shape of an eight-point star quilt block, dates to 1963.

Nevertheless, both paintings made the sale’s top ten list, slotting in at number eight for Stella and nine for Pollock, just above the second Frankenthaler. Other noteworthy results included Clyfford Still’s PH-589 (1959). Expected to sell for $4m to $6m, it hammered for $4.2m ($5.3m with fees) to an online bidder from Tel Aviv.

Leonardo Pertileâs book design for ADI Design Museumâs Compasso dâOro packs 1,040 pages into twin cloth volumes set in OT Marmo.

According to recent reports, compressing nearly seventy years of Italian industrial design into a 1,040-page brick isnât a subtle problem. Presented by Fondazione ADI, ADI Associazione per il Disegno Industriale, and ADI Design Museum, this Treccani monograph is edited by Beppe Finessi and designed by Leonardo Pertile as twin cloth editions. Brick-red cloth printed in royal blue marks the English Historical Collection with a yellow ribbon, while yellow cloth inked in red identifies the Italian Collezione Storica with a navy ribbon. Neither cover uses product photography. A large blind-debossed compass presses into the woven board under Omnitypeâs pre-release OT Marmo capitals, and opening the red cover flashes yellow endpaper beside three tall floor lamps.

According to the museumâs notes, the publication holds 2,275 images across three parts: ADI Design Museumâs archival role, the 1954â2022 Compasso dâOro Roll of Honour, and critical essays and interviews. Pertile keeps that scale legible by shifting the grid per section so the book design doesnât lose its rhythm. On pages 154 and 155, Anty Panseraâs essay wraps justified columns around four staggered black-and-white ceremony photos. Another spread runs a hand-drawn nebido logo study on millimeter graph paper across the top above justified prose and hanging-indent captions citing Franco Albini, Franca Helg, and Bob Noorda. Turn to pages 474 and 475 for Anno 1967 and the density jumps â Enzo Mariâs concentric Freud Opere sketches and Mario Piazzaâs ruled pull quote face Olivettiâs tight vertical matrix of color-coded marks.

Sources indicate that heavy catalogs donât work without quiet spreads. Page 577 pairs an overhead photo of a terracotta sofa and dark-green chaise directly above twin framed floor plans, leaving the plate clear of clutter. That open air widens in the essays and interviews. Alberto Saibeneâs Milano, 1954: cultura e industria opener floats OT Marmo headings high in white space above two narrow columns. On page 967, Beppe Finessiâs interview with Paola Antonelli switches to ragged-right text with outdented BF and PA initials in the margin so speakers scan fast. Itâs disciplined book design that makes a 1,040-page institutional archive easy to open and read.

6 Things I Learned While Hosting ‘The Design Drop’ Podcast

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1243 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When we rolled out The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear.
  • Sources indicate that as futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals.
  • What I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we rolled out The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear. Not the polished success stories or the advice you’ve heard a hundred times, but the mistakes, detours, and unspoken rules that don’t come with a job description.

Sources indicate that as futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals. So getting to sit down with designers, industry leaders, and a few unexpected voices to talk about what they’ve learned along the way? Pretty much my dream job.

What I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself. About careers, confidence, taking risks, and, yes, microphone stands.

After six episodes, here are the biggest lessons I’m taking away from my first season hosting The Design Drop podcast.

According to recent reports, when I talked to furniture designer Nicolai Czumaj-Bront, he shared how his career began at his kitchen table, after long days working as a consultant. No fancy studio or a perfectly mapped-out strategy. Just an idea, enough confidence to try it, and a willingness to invest in himself.

Twenty years later, he’s a senior design studio manager at Haworth.

Industry observers note that we spend so much time waiting until we feel qualified, prepared, or experienced enough to do something. But how are we supposed to get that experience if we never start? I’m trying to remind myself of this more often, especially when something feels outside my comfort zone.

Listen to Nicolai Czumaj-Bront’s full episode of The Design Drop, “In It, Not On It.”.

In a recent development, one of the most comforting discoveries of this experience? Even the people you look up to are still figuring things out.

It has been revealed that in my conversation with designer and entrepreneur Dan Mazzarini, we talked about the pressure to please everyone, especially when you’re building your career. But trying to be everything to everyone can mean losing sight of what makes your perspective valuable.

Confidence doesn’t necessarily mean having all the answers. Sometimes it means trusting yourself enough to stop looking for everyone else’s approval. And if the people you admire are still working through that, maybe you can give yourself a little grace, too.

Listen to Dan Mazzarini’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Professional People Pleasers.”.

Recent findings suggest that I’m a massive believer that everything happens for a reason, although it took me a while to get there. After talking to interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, I’m even more convinced that unexpected detours deserve a little more credit.

Caroline Murphy, host of The Design Drop podcast, with interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, who joined the show to discuss her unexpected career path and the opportunities that come from embracing change.

Sources indicate that clare didn’t set out to become a design influencer. Her career evolved from residential design into building her own content platform, back when becoming a design influencer wasn’t exactly an established career path.

It has been revealed that it got me thinking: How many of the best things in life have gone exactly according to plan? I’m going to guess… not many. Sometimes the side quest becomes the main quest. And sometimes the opportunity you almost passed up changes everything.

Listen to Clare Sullivan’s full episode of The Design Drop, “The Accidental Influencer.”.

This sounds contradictory, but stay with me. As we get older, life gets more complicated. Jobs, relationships, kids, pets, houses, bills—the list goes on. But we’re also gaining experience, perspective, and a better understanding of what matters.

Kay Sargent, senior principal and the director of thought leadership in HOK’s Interiors group, helped me see this differently. There are different seasons of life and work. You don’t have to be everything, everywhere, all at once. What deserves your energy today might look completely different five years from now.

I’m taking that as permission to stop expecting every part of life to be perfectly balanced.

Listen to Kay Sargent’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Everything Is a Season.”.

It has been revealed that my mom has a saying I’ve always loved: “Think of your 20s as data collection.” Every job, relationship, mistake, success, and questionable decision gives you information you didn’t have before. The point isn’t to get everything right. It’s to learn enough to make better decisions next time.

It has been revealed that my conversation with Jessica O. Matthews reinforced that idea. Jessica invented an energy-generating soccer ball at 19 and went on to build companies at the intersection of design, technology, and sustainability.

We talked about how much we can learn from experiences and perspectives outside our own industries. Not everything you learn has to fit neatly into your career path to be useful later. So, take the weird opportunity. Explore the random interest. Collect the data.

In a recent development, listen to Jessica O. Matthews’s full episode of The Design Drop, “No One Likes a Nepo Baby.”.

Every guest on The Design Drop brought something different to the conversation: different backgrounds, perspectives, and definitions of success.

Recent findings suggest that in my conversation with Kelly Cooper, a merchandising expert whose career has taken her through brands like Nike, Levi’s, and Universal Music Group, we talked about personal branding, advocating for yourself, and finding a version of success that actually works for you. That idea of defining success on your own terms really stuck with me.

We’re so busy comparing ourselves to other people that it’s easy to overlook what we’re uniquely good at. Sometimes it takes a mentor, colleague, or someone with a different perspective to help us recognize our strengths.

If you haven’t figured out your superpower yet, find people who will help you see it. And while you’re at it, be that person for someone else.

Listen to Kelly Cooper’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Do the Quiet Thing.”.

After six episodes of The Design Drop, I definitely don’t have all the answers—but I have more questions, newly introduced perspectives, and some pretty great advice to carry with me.

What surprised me most was how different everyone’s path looked, yet how much of the same challenges kept coming up. That’s what I hope this podcast can be: a place to talk about the stuff we’re all trying to figure out, with people who’ve been there (and often still are).

Thanks to our first six guests for being so open, and to everyone who’s listened along. Here’s to more conversations, unexpected lessons, and figuring things out as we go.

Sources indicate that all six episodes of The Design Drop are available on SURROUND and wherever you listen to podcasts. This season of The Design Drop is presented by Haworth.

As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, she develops community initiatives, programming, and recognition opportunities for Gen Z and early-career designers across brands including Interior Design, Metropolis, and LUXE Interiors + Design. A trained interior designer and graduate of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Murphy founded the Young Designers Collective in Nashville to help emerging designers learn, connect, and grow. Today, she's a speaker, connector, and self-described "Design Big Sister" dedicated to helping the emerging creatives find their place in the industry.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A candleholder has a relatively simple job: keep a candle upright. Beyond that, the possibilities are nearly endless. At Piscina, a contemporary collectible design gallery in Brooklyn’s Red Hook neighborhood, approximately 80 artists and designers have taken that freedom to heart, creating their own interpretations of the everyday object for a upcoming group exhibition.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Titled Candelabra Palaver, the exhibition opened Nov. 14, bringing together works selected through an open call. The brief was deliberately straightforward: make an object that holds a candle. With no prescribed materials, proportions, or aesthetic direction, participants could approach the assignment through their individual practices.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

The results explore just how much variation can emerge from a single functional requirement. Some contributors adhere to the familiar conventions of the candelabrum, while others push the object toward sculpture. Across the exhibition, differences in material, scale, and form reveal the many ways designers can interpret an object whose purpose has remained largely unchanged for centuries.

It has been revealed that candelabra by Fort Standard, featured in ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn. Photography courtesy of the artist and Piscina.

The exhibition’s title hints at its playful premise: Palaver refers to idle talk, conversation, or unnecessary fuss, an apt description for a gathering of creative voices offering different opinions on something as seemingly uncomplicated as a candleholder.

Sources indicate that participating studios include Fort Standard, Kin & Tech giant, Office of Tangible Spaces, Studio Daae, and Atelier Musset. Individual contributors include Sophie Collé, Steven Bukowski, Kaye Blegvad, Hanna Anonen, and Fitzhugh Karol, bringing together practitioners working across furniture, objects, art, and other creative disciplines.

In a recent development, candelabra by Hanna Anonen, featured in ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn. Photography courtesy of the artist and Piscina.

Click through the gallery above for a closer look at works featured in the exhibition.

The exhibition also reflects Piscina’s broader interest in the intersection of art, design, and craft. Founded in 2013 by artist and furniture designer Natalie Shook as a cooperative studio, Piscina has since evolved into a gallery and showroom dedicated to contemporary collectible design. Earlier this year, it introduced a dedicated gallery space alongside a reimagined showroom, expanding its platform for independent artists and designers.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Timed to coincide with the season of gatherings and candlelit evenings, Candelabra Palaver offers a reminder that even the most familiar household objects can provide fertile ground for experimentation. Whether restrained or exuberant, functional or sculptural, each piece begins with the same basic premise and arrives somewhere different.

Sources indicate that candelabra Palaver is on view until Dec. 31, 2026, at Piscina in Brooklyn, New York. All works in the exhibition are available for purchase.

Candelabra by Dustin Barzell, featured in ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn. Photography courtesy of the artist and Piscina.

Breaking: Should I Quit My Job? A Decision Framework

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • In a recent development, feeling frustrated on a Monday morning is not a reason to quit.
  • In a recent development, the FI community approaches this differently from mainstream career advice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

In a recent development, feeling frustrated on a Monday morning is not a reason to quit. But persistent patterns that affect your health, relationships, and long-term career growth are legitimate signals worth examining. The challenge is separating temporary frustration from genuine misalignment.

In a recent development, the FI community approaches this differently from mainstream career advice. Instead of asking "Am I happy at work?" — which fluctuates daily — we ask: "Is this role aligned with my long-term financial and personal goals?" That reframe turns an emotional decision into a strategic one.

Before you submit your resignation, your finances need to be ready regardless of how miserable you are. Quitting without financial preparation trades one source of stress for another.

The FI community has a massive advantage here. If you have been building toward financial independence — even if you are not there yet — your savings provide a runway that most people do not have. A $200,000 investment portfolio at a 4% safe withdrawal rate provides $8,000 per year in sustainable income, which dramatically reduces the pressure of a job search.

It has been revealed that the worst time to make a career decision is when you are emotionally overwhelmed. A terrible meeting, a passed-over promotion, or a toxic interaction with a coworker can make quitting feel urgent when the situation may actually be temporary or fixable.

It has been revealed that use the 30-day test: if you have wanted to quit for fewer than 30 consecutive days, it is likely a temporary frustration. If the feeling has persisted — or intensified — for 30+ days, it is a pattern worth taking seriously.

Industry observers note that how you leave a job matters as much as why you leave. Your professional reputation follows you for your entire career, and the people you work with today may be the hiring managers, clients, or references of tomorrow.

Two weeks notice: This is the minimum professional standard in the United States. For senior roles, three to four weeks is more appropriate. Check your employment contract — some roles require 30, 60, or 90 days notice.

The resignation conversation: Schedule a private meeting with your direct manager. Keep it brief and positive. Say: "I have decided to move on to a latest opportunity. I want to thank you for [specific positive thing], and I am committed to making the transition as smooth as possible. My last day would be [date].".

Recent findings suggest that the transition plan: Document your ongoing projects, key contacts, passwords, and processes. Offer to train your replacement. Complete as much outstanding work as possible. A strong exit creates goodwill that pays dividends for years.

What not to do: Do not badmouth the company, your boss, or your coworkers — not in the resignation meeting, not in your exit interview, not on social media. Even if your grievances are legitimate, airing them publicly hurts your reputation more than theirs.

Conventional advice notes never quit without another job lined up. The FI community takes a more nuanced view: it depends on your financial position and the severity of the situation.

According to recent reports, if you are leaving due to tech giant changes — layoffs, restructuring, or role elimination — negotiate your severance package. Many employees accept the first offer without realizing severance is negotiable. Key leverage points include your tenure, difficulty of replacement, willingness to sign a non-compete or non-disparagement clause, and any outstanding commissions or bonuses.

Common severance components to negotiate: extended pay (push for 2-4 weeks per year of tenure), continued health insurance coverage, outplacement services, vesting acceleration for equity, and a positive reference commitment.

Sources indicate that health insurance is often the biggest financial concern when leaving a job. You have two primary options:.

Sources indicate that COBRA: Continues your employer proposal for up to 18 months. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer was paying) plus a 2% administrative fee. COBRA typically costs $500-$700 per month for individual coverage and $1,400-$2,000+ for family coverage. It is expensive but familiar.

ACA Marketplace: Depending on your income after leaving, you may qualify for substantial subsidies. If your annual income drops below 400% of the federal poverty level, premium tax credits can reduce your monthly cost to $100-$400 for comprehensive coverage. FI seekers who leave jobs often qualify for significant subsidies because their earned income drops even if their net worth is high — ACA subsidies are based on income, not wealth.

Sources indicate that here is where financial independence changes everything. When you have significant savings — even if you have not reached full FI — you have leverage that most employees lack. You can negotiate from strength, take career risks, and walk away from toxic situations without financial desperation.

A $500,000 portfolio at a 4% withdrawal rate provides $20,000 per year indefinitely. That is not enough to live on for most people, but combined with a working spouse, reduced expenses, or part-time work, it transforms "should I quit my job" from a terrifying question into a strategic calculation. FI is not just about never working again — it is about having the financial security to make career decisions based on alignment and purpose rather than desperation and fear.

Sources indicate that the FI community has a saying: financial independence is not about quitting your job — it is about having the freedom to choose whether to keep it. Every dollar you save and invest is a vote for your future autonomy. When you have 12-24 months of expenses saved, you negotiate from strength. When you reach Coast FI or beyond, a bad job becomes a choice, not a trap. Build your FI runway and the question changes from "Can I afford to quit?" to "Does this role still serve my goals?".

Work through these steps before making your decision.

Industry observers note that have you consistently wanted to leave for 30+ days? If no, wait. Temporary frustration is not a reason to upend your career. If yes, proceed to step two.

In a recent development, pro tip: Keep a brief daily journal noting your satisfaction level 1-10. Data beats feelings for decision-making.

Is the matter your boss, your role, your compensation, the culture, or the industry? Some problems follow you to the next job. A bad manager is fixable by transferring. An industry you hate requires a bigger change.

Verify your emergency fund, health insurance options, debt situation, and FI runway. If you are not financially ready, keep working while you build your safety net and search for alternatives.

Industry observers note that before quitting, have you requested a transfer, a raise, a role change, or a conversation with HR? Many solvable problems go unaddressed because employees assume the answer will be no.

Pro tip: A direct conversation with your manager about your concerns resolves the matter 40% of the time.

If you decide to leave, secure your next opportunity (if possible), give appropriate notice, document your work for your successor, and maintain every professional relationship.

Pro tip: Never burn bridges. The colleague you leave today may be the hiring manager at your dream manufacturer in three years.

At minimum, 3-6 months of essential expenses in a liquid savings account. If you are quitting without another job lined up, aim for 6-12 months. The FI community recommends having your emergency fund fully funded, health insurance secured, and ideally some progress toward financial independence to provide a psychological safety net.

If your job is causing persistent anxiety, depression, or physical health symptoms that do not improve with coping strategies, therapy, or workplace changes — yes, your health must come first. But do it strategically: secure health insurance, build your financial runway, and consult a therapist or career coach before making the leap. Never make a permanent career decision during a temporary emotional crisis.

Generally, quitting gives you more control over the narrative, timing, and terms. Being fired can qualify you for unemployment benefits (quitting usually does not), but it can also create a negative reference. If you sense a termination is coming, consider whether negotiating a mutual separation with severance is an option. Document everything and consult an employment attorney if you believe the termination may be discriminatory or retaliatory.

Be honest and frame it positively. Acceptable explanations include: career transition (took time to retrain or earn a certification), personal development (traveled, volunteered, or cared for family), or strategic job search (took time to find the right fit rather than settling). Employers increasingly accept career gaps — especially post-2020 — as long as you can articulate what you did during the time off.

COBRA (Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) lets you continue your employer health strategy for up to 18 months after leaving. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer contributed) plus a 2% admin fee. Individual coverage typically costs $500-$700/month and family coverage runs $1,400-$2,000+/month. The ACA marketplace is often cheaper, especially if your income drops after leaving.

FI savings transform the equation entirely. With a substantial portfolio, you have a financial runway that removes the urgency and desperation from the decision. Even partial FI — having 2-5 years of expenses invested — means you can quit a toxic job, take time to find the right next role, or transition to lower-paying but more fulfilling work. FI is not just about retiring early; it is about having the leverage to make career decisions from a position of strength rather than fear.

According to recent reports, the question "should I quit my job?" deserves a framework, not an impulse. Apply the 30-day test, diagnose the real problem, verify your financial readiness, explore internal solutions, and then make a deliberate decision. If you have been building toward financial independence, your savings give you something most people lack: the freedom to walk away from a bad situation without financial panic. FI is the ultimate career insurance — it turns "I have to stay" into "I choose to stay or go." Build your runway, protect your reputation, and make the decision from a position of strength.
