📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Emily Carr and E.J. Hughes lead the way at Heffel's $10m autumn auctions

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Heffel Fine Art Auction House held its marquee autumn evening sales on Wednesday (18 November) in Toronto, attracting a packed house of bidders and spectators to the city’s swank Yorkville district and generating C$14.4m ($10m) in sales, works by Canadian masters taking top dollar.
  • “At a time of strong national pride, it is especially meaningful to see collectors celebrating Canada’s artistic achievements and our distinct national culture,” David Heffel, the auction house’s president, mentioned at the end of the evening.
  • Heffel's evening auctions in Toronto on 18 November Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Heffel Fine Art Auction House held its marquee autumn evening sales on Wednesday (18 November) in Toronto, attracting a packed house of bidders and spectators to the city’s swank Yorkville district and generating C$14.4m ($10m) in sales, works by Canadian masters taking top dollar. As things got underway, a Heffel representative noted that any US tariffs were “the responsibility of the buyer”, a reflection of these often-testy times.

“At a time of strong national pride, it is especially meaningful to see collectors celebrating Canada’s artistic achievements and our distinct national culture,” David Heffel, the auction house’s president, mentioned at the end of the evening.

Heffel's evening auctions in Toronto on 18 November Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

Sources indicate that the back-to-back sales (41 lots of post-war and contemporary art followed by 47 works of Canadian, Impressionist and modern art) got off to a flying start when a watercolour by the Vancouver-born artist E.J. Hughes hammered for C$475,000 ($331,700)—nearly 12 times its high estimate. Titled Wharves at Chemainus (2000) and depicting the titular logging community on Vancouver Island, the painting is modest in size at 20in by 24in; with fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900).

According to recent reports, hughes had made waves at Heffel’s auctions last spring, when his Coastal Boats Near Sidney, BC realised a whoppingC$5.7m ($4.1m), including fees. Several more Hughes works were up for sale Wednesday night including two that significantly outperformer their estimates: The Hope River at Chilliwack, BC (1961), which took in C$253,250 ($176,800) with fees; and The Freighter “World Ares” at Crofton (1980), which hauled in C$229,250 ($160,000) including fees.

Emily Carr, Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure), around 1912 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

The second sale’s cover lot, Emily Carr’s luminous canvas Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure) (around 1912), brought C$1.3m ($922,000) including fees, comfortably within its estimate. It was the only seven-figure result of the night. Some of the proceeds from its sale will benefit the Audain Art Museum in Whistler, British Columbia, where it was shown in the context of a major traveling exhibition of Carr’s work in 2019-20.

It has been revealed that A work on paper by the Carr, Music in the Trees (around 1935), topped its high estimate to achieve an impressive C$421,250 ($294,100) with fees. In all, six works by the Victoria-born artist were sold at Heffel on Wednesday night, fetching a combined, fee-inclusive total of C$2.5m ($1.7m).

Jean Paul Riopelle, Herbeuse, 1967 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

A handful of works by Jean Paul Riopelle were on offer during the post-war and contemporary portion of the night, generating around C$1.3m ($907,800) in sales. His large-scale, wintry abstraction Herbeuse (1967),proved particularly appealing. Swift bidding pushed it to around double its high estimate. With fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900). It was shown in the Carnegie International the year Riopelle painted it, and later in Paris, where the Montréal-born artist, a master of the palette knife, spent decades. The work with the highest estimate in the post-war and contemporary sale, Riopelle’s Brumaire (1953), was expected to bring between C$1.5m and C$2m, but failed to sell.

Among the night’s other significant-ticket items was Paul-Émile Borduas’s oil painting Empâtement (1957), from the artist’s black-and-white period—and punctuated with splashes of red. It realised C$841,250 with fees ($587,400), easily topping its high estimate of C$500,000. It had been acquired directly from the artist by London’s Arthur Tooth & Sons gallery in 1957 and, more recently, was in the collection of Québecois lyricist and songwriter Luc Plamondon.

Paul-Émile Borduas, Empâtement, 1957 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

It has been revealed that J.E.H. MacDonald’s oil sketch Magnetawan River Rapids (1912), a preparatory work for a major canvas that is in the collection of the Art Gallery of Hamilton, achieved C$451,250 with fees ($315,000), tripling its high estimate of C$150,000.

In a recent development, arguably the surprise of the night was Ivan Eyre (1935-2022), who was long a professor at the University of Manitoba and is best known for his prairie landscapes. His intensely autumnal acrylic-on-canvas landscape Golden Rod (1981) realised C$391,250 with fees ($273,200), more than tripling its high estimate of C$120,000 while setting a latest auction record for the artist. That record was smashed in turn just one lot later, when Eyre’s Yellow Wood (around 1995) realised C$481,250 with fees ($336,000), five times its high estimate of C$90,000.

Ivan Eyre, Golden Rod, 1981 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

The beloved William Kurelek, who was raised on a farm near Winnipeg, also made a splash.His snowy landscape painting I Knew How the Clouds Arise (1969), which was featured on the cover of the catalogue for the artist’s first retrospective in 1970, realised C$313,250 including fees ($218,700), just over its high estimate, while the evocative campfire scene Wiener Roast on My Father’s Farm (1974), exceeded expectations to sell for C$265,250 with fees ($185,200).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Photographer Ahmed al-Bekkar fled Syria more than a decade ago, seeking refuge in Turkey amid widespread destruction, looting, and attacks by the terrorist group ISIS (Daesh) and forces loyal to Syria’s now-topled Assad regime, according to a report by Anadolu Agency.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Syrian photographer has finally been reunited with his personal photo archive more than a decade after hiding it behind a wall he built during the country’s war.

Photographer Ahmed al-Bekkar fled Syria more than a decade ago, seeking refuge in Turkey amid widespread destruction, looting, and attacks by the terrorist group ISIS (Daesh) and forces loyal to Syria’s now-topled Assad regime, according to a report by Anadolu Agency.

‘Every piece of paper has a history, every page holds a memory’.

🇸🇾 Syrian photographer Ahmed al-Bekkar recovers personal archive in Raqqa after more than a decade.

● Bekkar, 66, sealed his library before fleeing war to protect books, photographs and personal documents.

● He sought refuge in Türkiye amid attacks by Daesh (ISIS) and forces of ousted Syrian regime.

— Anadolu English (@anadoluagency) November 19, 2026.

Industry observers note that before leaving Syria, Bekkar built a wall to conceal the entrance to his personal library in the northern city of Raqqa, hoping to protect his extensive photographic archive. The archive contains approximately 3,000 printed photographs of Raqqa, as well as a much larger digital collection documenting historical sites, cities, and markets across Syria.

During his decade in Turkey, the now 66-year-old photographer continued his photographic work, helping establish the House of Migrants association and the Turkish-Arab Art House. Although Bekkar spent productive years doing photography in the Turkish capital of Istanbul, he says nothing could replace his hometown in Syria.

Sources indicate that anadolu Agency reports that Bekkar returned to Raqqa this year and reopened the library he had concealed behind the wall more than a decade earlier. The photographer describes watching the bricks being removed one by one from the wall as an emotional experience, having long dreamed of setting foot inside his archive again.

Recent findings suggest that “Every piece of paper has a history, every page holds a memory. I spent time and effort obtaining and preserving every document,” the photographer tells the news outlet. “I feel that those days are preserved in these papers, whose owners are no longer with us, but which have remained behind.”.

Bekkar recalled growing up across from an old mosque in Raqqa, where the surrounding historical buildings inspired his interest in photography and Syria’s cultural heritage. Since returning to his hometown, Bekkar has revisited historical sites he photographed years earlier to document them now.

Meet Harry Nuriev, Bjarke Ingels' pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1574 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Jenia Filatova unless stated.
  • In a recent development, BIG founder Bjarke Ingels has selected Harry Nuriev for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler.
  • Nuriev established his studio, Crosby Studios, 12 years ago with the aim of shaking up the world of interior design.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Jenia Filatova unless stated.

In a recent development, BIG founder Bjarke Ingels has selected Harry Nuriev for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, the Latest York and Paris-based designer explains how he constantly aims to reinvent himself and his work.

Nuriev established his studio, Crosby Studios, 12 years ago with the aim of shaking up the world of interior design.

“First, it came from this game of rejection,” he told Dezeen from his house in Tuscany.

Sources indicate that “Let’s say everyone likes to use wood – I won’t have any wood. If everyone likes beige or brown – I won’t have beige or brown. People are confused with a material, so that’s exactly the material I’m going to use.”.

In a recent development, “I’ll bring exterior to interior, interior to exterior,” he continued. “I’ll mess everything. My colours will be inspired by fashion, my texture will be inspired by architecture.”.

It has been revealed that “You can’t be safe. You always have to risk.”.

Recent findings suggest that over a decade later, the strategy appears to have worked. Nuriev was recently named Designer of the Year at French design show Maison&Objet and has a client list that many designers would envy. Among his recent works are a sofa for Balenciaga, a pop-up store for Skims, a reflecting pool for Gucci and a puffer-jacket-filled virtual sofa for Nike.

Now Ingels, arguably the world’s best known architect, has selected him as the designer that he believes will have the biggest impact over the next 20 years, as part of our fresh series marking 20 years of Dezeen.

Nuriev established his own studio after freelancing and working on other people’s projects for many years, with the aim of being able to pursue his own creative interests.

“When you work freelance just to pay bills, you don’t really have particular voice,” he stated. “You have nothing really too specific to express.”.

“I was like, hold on, I actually need to pull all the things together to express myself, whether it’s comfortable for everyone or not.”.

At the time he established his studio, Nuriev recalls the interior design landscape being constrained and dominated by a couple of key, predominant styles that he was determined to break out of.

Industry observers note that “Twelve years ago interior design was just minimalistic Japanese style or classic,” he mentioned. “Maybe there were some alternative, very vague and obscure styles, but there was literally just two, maybe two and a half camps.”.

“I remember that in interior design, and in particular the industrial area, there was no room to express yourself in a fashion or an art way,” he continued.

According to recent reports, “[I realised] there is no way that everyone needs to live the same way, have the same living room and sit in the same sofa. I thought that I will create something different.”.

It was really a substantial experiment. In retrospect, looking back now, I really think I was lucky.

Rather than identify a target market or clients that wanted a particular style, Nuriev simply set out to create his own individually styled interior spaces and objects.

“It was really a major experiment,” he said. “In retrospect, looking back now, I really think I was lucky.”.

“By then I had learned classic and traditional way of doing it, so I knew the marble game and wood game and all of the, let’s say, Architectural Digest alphabet. But my idea was that my personal voice, my internal conversation, was very different, I didn’t know if people would like it or not,” he continued.

“Then, to my surprise, some people liked it.”.

It has been revealed that much of Crosby Studio’s work utilises stainless steel, and has an appearance that is cold and almost uncomfortable. However, although this aesthetic is now associated with the studio, Nuriev is keen to ensure that his work continues to evolve.

“I understand we’re responsible for this whole stainless steel, futuristic, uncomfortable, Instagramable aesthetic,” he mentioned.

“In a certain way we keep in our DNA our signature things that people already liked, even though they’re kind of retired for me and maybe I want something different,” he continued.

But we always experiment because that’s the part of the formula, part of the recipe, to always have this little spice in every project.

“But we always experiment because that’s the part of the formula, part of the recipe, to always have this little spice in every project.”.

His metallic, almost cold aesthetic is partly born of the idea that you can create spaces that people can be enjoy without necessarily being comfortable.

“It’s bullshit because there’s no such a thing [as comfort],” he stated. “I remember after a nightclub at 2am, sitting on a sidewalk, eating some hot dog and being extremely happy, but also I remember being in the most refined, beautiful restaurant, sitting in the most comfortable chair with soft cushioning and feel miserable.”.

“I developed this mentality that comfort is actually not really healthy,” he continued. “Sitting comfortably in a sort of like sleeping environment, where you can relax all the way, can pull the strength out of you.”.

The competition to create something upcoming and attention-grabbing has intensified in the past 10 years, but Nuriev believes that it is still possible to find new ways of reinventing materials and forms through a process of experimentation and reinvention that he calls “transformism”.

“[I tell myself] ‘don’t fool yourself, you can’t create anything new, Harry,'” he noted. “What you can do, you can find an existing thing and you can reinvent it. You can find a new life.”.

“I’m trying to find newly introduced materials, and it’s becoming harder and harder because we explore quite a lot of different things, but surprisingly, there is always something,” he continued.

“It’s like music – every year there is upcoming songs, there is new combinations of the same notes that we have known since Mozart, Bach and Chopin, but it’s still different.”.

After more than a decade, Nuriev has a clear idea of his and Crosby Studio’s strengths, as well as the limitations of his creations.

“They are dessert-ish in their nutrition level, kind of like the entertaining side,” he stated. “You don’t expect a full meal from Crosby.”.

Recent findings suggest that “You come to experience emotion,” he continued. “You want to have this sweet or salty or spicy something, and then you get it and you go. It’s not a daily situation.”.

He believes that his work translates best at the medium scale – an installation, store, room or hotel lobby.

My nightmare is to become a replica of my own self and just retire, becoming an established artist who just found his own voice and just puts his signature everywhere.

Recent findings suggest that “I think I have found my scale,” he said. “We work in major development projects, which is fine. We can deliver it easily, but there are so many great people who can do it better than us.”.

“Rather than we just distribute all our juice everywhere, and then maybe it will have less energy, [for example in] a huge building, let’s just do this lobby so crazy that people will feel the emotion.”.

As Crosby Studios has established its reputation, the profile of its clients has risen considerably to include some extremely well known and demanding brands, though Nuriev says these projects can be the most creative.

“The calibre of clients is changing dramatically,” he mentioned. “And you know it’s just like in a computer game, you feel like you’re on a different level, they speak in different vocabulary, it’s just complete different game.”.

“Now I’m working with big sharks, and obviously their expectation is different. They’ve been working before me with bigger artists, so it’s also challenging. But this is the challenge of growing.”.

Nuriev believes his most important role at Crosby Studios now is to maintain the “rebellious spirit” that it was introduced with – something that inevitably becomes harder as a studio grows and the clients change.

“I think the game now is to constantly remind myself that we’re not an Armani Casa with steel, no matter how old we are, and to keep this spirit,” he noted.

“I think that’s my job as the founder to remind my team, yes, we have gained professional skills, we know how to talk to people, we know how to draft a contract, we know how to deliver on time, but nevertheless, we still want to keep our rebellious spirit.”.

His biggest fear? Becoming a pastiche of himself and rolling out designs in an unchanging signature style.

“My nightmare is to become a replica of my own self and just retire, becoming an established artist who just found his own voice and just puts his signature everywhere. This is not what I want.”.

“As Coco Chanel remarked, once you feel comfortable, it’s the time to change completely. So to reinvent yourself is an exercise, and it’s pretty much my daily life.”.

Sources indicate that to celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

Photography by Jenia Filatova unless stated.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photographers can save hundreds of dollars on an expansive range of Sony mirrorless cameras, from budget-friendly APS-C models all the way to flagship full-frame bodies.

Recent findings suggest that starting with the APS-C camera deals, photographers can save $50 on Sony’s best APS-C interchangeable-lens model, the a6700. With its 26-megapixel Exmor R BSI CMOS sensor and 4Kp120 recording, the a6700 is a versatile and fully featured camera. While there’s no instant discount on it right now, unlike the rest of the cameras in this story, there is a $50 cashback campaign running through December 31, 2026. The camera is $1,498, but the $50 back later is nice.

Sources indicate that with the 24.2-megapixel Sony ZV-E10, which comes in both black and white colorways, the $50 savings is upfront. The video-focused camera, designed for content creators, is $748 thanks to ongoing holiday savings. That's $450 less than its successor, the ZV-E10 II, which costs $1,198 and isn't discounted. That's big savings.

Industry observers note that the Sony a6400 isn't quite as advanced as the a6700, but the 24-megapixel model remains a very capable APS-C mirrorless camera. It's also significantly more accessible, especially after its $200 instant holiday discount. At $898, this is among the best values in Sony's APS-C lineup.

Recent findings suggest that on the full-frame side of things, there are a ton of great discounts right now, including up to $600 off a Sony a7 III. While it has been succeeded by the a7 IV and, most recently, the a7 V, the Sony a7 III is still a capable camera, able to capture high-quality 24-megapixel photos and 4Kp30 video. At $1,398 after its $600 discount, it's the most affordable way into a new Sony full-frame camera right now. There's also a $50 cashback campaign for this camera.

Speaking of the newer a7 IV, that's on sale, too. In fact, it's $500 off—plus the $50 cashback campaign. It's $1,998 today before the $50 back later. It has a 33-megapixel sensor, 4Kp60 video recording, and some autofocus bells and whistles its predecessor lacks.

Well, the even newer a7 V is on sale, too! The discount is a bit smaller at just $200, plus $50 back after purchase, but it's still something. The Sony a7 V is great. It missed out on PetaPixel's Camera of the Year Award last year by a single point.

Sources indicate that on the other end of Sony's full-frame camera lineup, the former flagship Sony a1 is $5,698 after a $500 discount. Then there's $50 back later with proof of purchase until the end of the year. While the a1 II is naturally an even better camera, a lot of pros are still using the original a1 to do incredible work.

It has been revealed that on the topic of the excellent Sony a1 II, that's also on sale. However, even with its $200 discount, it is still $6,798, which is obviously quite a bit more than the original a1. It's an expensive flagship camera, but it is undeniably fantastic. It's the best Sony has to offer.

Sources indicate that while the 66-megapixel Sony a7R VI is the talk of the high-resolution town these days, it would be a major mistake to look past its predecessor, the Sony a7R V. The a7R V remains an excellent camera, and at $3,298 thanks to $500 in holiday savings (plus $50 back later), it's a superb value. For reference, the a7R VI is $4,498 before $50 cash back. What are the extra megapixels and added speed worth to you? Landscape and portrait photographers, in particular, may very well find the a7R V more than sufficient.

In a recent development, if you don't like the SLR styling of the a7R V but still want its 61-megapixel image sensor, there's always the a7CR. With its compact form factor and stylish black and silver color choices, the a7CR offers the same image quality as the a7R V without the bulk. It's $400 off and is also part of Sony's cashback campaign. At $2,998, it's an attractive option.

Industry observers note that the a7CR's similarly styled sibling, the 33-megapixel a7C II, is $400 off, too. With that discount, it's down to $2,098 right now.

It has been revealed that if megapixels don't tickle your fancy but speed does, the Sony a9 III is $400 off for the holidays. Sony's first, and thus far only, global-shutter Alpha camera, the 24-megapixel a9 III is screaming fast. It shoots full-resolution photos with autofocus at up to 120 frames per second, has literally zero rolling shutter, and is built with professionals in mind. It's still $6,398, so the speed doesn't come cheap, but boy, is it ever fast.

It has been revealed that the video-focused Sony a7S III might never get a successor, [although we hope it does](https://petapixel.com/2026/09/29/is-a-sony-a7s-iv-coming-fat-chance/), but that doesn't mean the a7S III is bad. Far from it. It remains a great camera for video applications, especially in low-light conditions. It's $3,698 after a $300 discount.

Another video-focused model, the content-creator-friendly ZV-E1, is $300 off right now. Available in black and white colorways, the 12-megapixel camera is very good at video. That discount knocks its price down to $2,198.

While you don't need a Sony memory card for your Sony camera, there are some good deals on Sony Tough cards right now.

Recent findings suggest that the excellent Tough Series UHS-II SDXC memory cards are discounted for the holidays. The 64GB version is $45 off, bringing it down to $133. The 128GB model is $100 off, making it $243. Finally, the 256GB card is $120 off, which means it's $418 right now.

Some of Sony's high-end cameras also use CFexpress Type A cards. A few of those are on sale, too, including $60 off Sony's 960GB CFexpress 4.0 Type A Tough card. It's still $878, though. The 1920GB version is $140 off, which makes it $1,458. Memory card prices have gone wild lately. Unfortunately, the 240GB and 480GB cards aren't discounted right now.

#80110. Adobe Ends Free Creative Cloud Subscriptions for Stock Photographers

Adobe Ends Free Creative Cloud Subscriptions for Stock Photographers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (412 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Adobe will no longer offer complimentary Creative Cloud subscriptions to photographers who sell their work through Adobe Stock, replacing the scheme with discounts instead.
  • For years, Adobe has incentivized photographers to contribute to its picture marketplace by dangling the carrot of a free subscription to Photoshop and other Adobe apps.
  • Robert Kneschke, a professional stock photographer based in Germany who runs the Daily Life of a Photo Producer blog, says that in 2020, a photographer needed 150 sales to unlock a free Adobe Photography proposal, while 5,000 downloads would net them complete access to Creative Cloud.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Adobe will no longer offer complimentary Creative Cloud subscriptions to photographers who sell their work through Adobe Stock, replacing the scheme with discounts instead.

For years, Adobe has incentivized photographers to contribute to its picture marketplace by dangling the carrot of a free subscription to Photoshop and other Adobe apps.

Robert Kneschke, a professional stock photographer based in Germany who runs the Daily Life of a Photo Producer blog, says that in 2020, a photographer needed 150 sales to unlock a free Adobe Photography proposal, while 5,000 downloads would net them complete access to Creative Cloud.

Industry observers note that but Adobe has recently made changes to its bonus program, changing the eligibility and prizes. Instead of offering full complimentary access, Adobe is offering a 70% discount on Creative Cloud Pro to the first 500 contributors who generate 6,500 downloads and submit over 1,000 new images.

The 70% discount is also on offer to the first 500 contributors who “have 10 or more datasets and maintain high quality standards.” It’s not entirely clear what a dataset is from a photographer’s perspective. On its website, Adobe describes it as a “storage and management construct for a collection of data, typically a table, that contains a schema (columns) and fields (rows).”.

There’s also a 40% discount on offer for Creative Cloud Pro for the first 10,000 contributors who generate more than 2,500 sales as well as submitting over “100 pieces of unique content.”.

In a recent development, the above criteria must be met from September 22, 2026, to March 12, 2027. The codes will be handed out in April.

Adobe will still provide full complimentary access to Creative Cloud Pro to photographers who are “actively commissioned to create content and/or require Adobe tools to fulfill project requirements.”.

Writing on his blog, Kneschke calls the changes a “clear step backward” while speculating that the datasets are for AI training purposes.

Industry observers note that “A gift has become a discount voucher,” Kneschke says. “Along with the lower royalties, this is further evidence that Adobe is cutting costs at the expense of photographers.”.

Earlier this year, PetaPixel reported on Gerald Carter, the owner of Diversity Photos, and his fight with Adobe after he discovered that the manufacturer trained its AI image generator Firefly on his entire photo library.

Three Photographers Sue Police Over Use of Tear Gas and Pepper Spray During ICE Raid

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that three photographers have sued the St.
  • Warning: The following photos contains content that some may find upsetting.
  • Aaron Nesheim, a photographer for Sahan Journal, MPR News photojournalist Kerem Yücel, and freelance photographer Timothy Evans filed the lawsuit against the St.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that three photographers have sued the St. Paul Police Department in Minnesota over its alleged use of chemical munitions against them during an ICE raid, with their own photographs documenting the incident.

Warning: The following photos contains content that some may find upsetting.

Aaron Nesheim, a photographer for Sahan Journal, MPR News photojournalist Kerem Yücel, and freelance photographer Timothy Evans filed the lawsuit against the St. Paul Police Department on Tuesday. The photographers accuse officers of firing pepper balls at them, pepper-spraying them at close range, and deploying tear gas against them while they were covering a demonstration.

Sources indicate that the lawsuit stems from an incident on November 25 last year, when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents attempted to arrest a man at his home in the Payne-Phalen neighborhood of St. Paul, Minnesota. A growing crowd of protesters gathered outside the property as federal agents attempted to detain the man.

Nesheim, Yücel, and Evans arrived at the scene to document the protest. All three photographers carried large professional cameras and wore press passes around their necks. Evans also wore a ballistic vest labeled “PRESS.”.

Sources indicate that according to a report by the Minnesota Reformer, St. Paul police officers also responded to the scene. After ICE agents left with the detainees, protesters demanded that local police leave as well. As the officers withdrew, they fired pepper balls and used pepper spray and tear gas against both protesters and photojournalists.

Industry observers note that according to court documents, an officer pepper-sprayed Yücel at close range while he was photographing the scene. The lawsuit says that the photographer inhaled and swallowed the chemicals. Other officers fired pepper balls at Yücel, striking him in the neck, shoulders, and chest.

According to the complaint, the three photographers were standing together off to the side of the crowd, at least 10 feet from the nearest protesters and out of the way of law enforcement officers. Despite this, police allegedly fired pepper balls and launched tear gas at the photographers.

In a recent development, all three photographers experienced irritation to their eyes and airways following exposure to the chemicals. Yücel struggled to breathe and was taken from the scene by ambulance. According to MPR News, Yücel was forced to put his jacket into a garbage bag to prevent the chemicals from affecting the crew and staff at Regions Hospital said they could not admit Yücel into the main hospital because the chemical irritants on his body and clothing posed a safety risk to staff and other patients.

According to recent reports, evans suffered severe abdominal bruising after a pepper ball exploded inside his ballistic vest, while Nesheim was struck in the head by a police projectile. All three photojournalists required mental health treatment following the incident.

The photographers argue in their lawsuit that the St. Paul Police Department’s actions violated their rights under the First, Fourth, and Fourteenth Amendments of the U.S. Constitution and constituted assault and battery, among other violations. They are seeking damages, attorney’s fees, and a court order barring the St. Paul Police Department from engaging in further unconstitutional conduct against them.

Recent findings suggest that “The use of this tear gas, like the use of the pepper balls, was clearly meant as retaliation for plaintiffs’ exercise of their First Amendment rights,”attorney Kevin Riach writes. “The officers could not have been shooting at anyone other than Nesheim, Yücel and Evans, who were all clustered within several feet of one another.”.

#80106. Johnson Banks Unveils the RIBA brand identity

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (451 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abduzeedo ↗ Open Full Page

Johnson Banks Unveils the RIBA brand identity

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (451 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abduzeedo

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Johnson Banks rebuilds RIBA for its 200th birthday: the RIBA brand identity turns negative space into a bold typographic mark.
  • It has been revealed that the first thing you see is the space between the letters.
  • Johnson Banks started from a Philip Johnson line, that all great architecture is the design of space that contains, cuddles, exalts, or stimulates the people in that space, and let the negative space inside the four letters carry the idea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Johnson Banks rebuilds RIBA for its 200th birthday: the RIBA brand identity turns negative space into a bold typographic mark.

It has been revealed that the first thing you see is the space between the letters. RIBA arrives as four solid capitals on a pale wall, each letter built from the gaps around it, the R split into a bowl and a leg, the B into two stacked bowls, the A into a triangle over a flat base. It is a mark about architecture made from architecture itself, walls and openings rather than a drawn symbol, and it holds at every size, from a tote bag to a building banner.

The type does the work. Johnson Banks started from a Philip Johnson line, that all great architecture is the design of space that contains, cuddles, exalts, or stimulates the people in that space, and let the negative space inside the four letters carry the idea. The mark can sit on top of a photograph, cut into it, or anchor a corner or an edge, and the same logic runs through a set of drop capitals, letters drawn to open a page like a doorway.

It has been revealed that the old identity, letters drawn by Eric Gill beside a highly detailed symbol, had drifted over twenty-five years into hundreds of sub-brands with no house style holding them together. The new system pulls them back into line, with related identities for RSAW, the Royal Society of Architects in Wales, and RIBAJ, the institute journal, each sitting inside the same approach, and clear guidelines built on accessible fonts so the brand stays useful and durable.

In a recent development, colour went back to the beginning. The historic red, the shade the public knows from RIBA signboards, returns front and centre, running across the tote bag, the drawing stencil and the vertical banner on a brick facade. Against it, the palette stays quiet, stone grey, pale blue, black, so the red reads as a signal rather than a decoration, and the crest, the two lions, survives in a simplified, softened form as a quiet sign-off, debossed in black on black.

The system proves itself on the objects architects use. Book spines carry RIBA, RSAW and RIBAJ in red, white and blue on a wooden shelf. A red stencil ruler cuts the letters into a drawing tool. A poster for the Domestic Building Contract pairs a giant yellow D with a red architectural photograph. And the illustration style, flat geometric shapes in red, blue and green with small cut-out figures, gives the brand a way to talk about people without a photograph.

#80104. Christie’s tepid 21st-century sale caps week of blockbuster auctions in Fresh York

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1658 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Christie’s tepid 21st-century sale caps week of blockbuster auctions in Fresh York

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1658 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in New York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees).
  • Just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%.
  • Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in New York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees). That tally fell short of Christie’s pre-sale expectations, which do not account for fees, and projected a total take in the range of $126m to $192m. It was also a lower result compared to the auction house’s last two equivalent sales in New York—namely the $132m ($162.6m with fees) generated across 42 lots last May, and the $99.5m ($123.5m with fees) brought by 45 lots one year ago.

Just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%. Two lots were withdrawn at the last moment, including a Jeff Koons sculpture estimated to bring between $3m and $5m. Twenty-four lots were backed by third-party guarantees and nine were backed fully by house guarantees, representing around 59% of all the works offered. Auction records for three artists were broken over the course of the night.

Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Business began with a bang at Christie’s Rockefeller Center salesroom: the first lot was Roy Lichtenstein’s Small Wall Explosion (1965), executed in porcelain enamel on steel and perforated steel relief to mimic the Ben-Day dot style from his paintings. It sold to a telephone bidder for $625,000 ($800,000 with fees). From an edition of six, it hailed from the collection of Antonio Homem Sonnabend, the adopted son of the late and legendary dealer and collector Ileana Sonnabend (1914-2007) and who ran his mother’s namesake gallery in its waning years. Antonio Homem died earlier this year, at age 86.

Another of the 19 Sonnabend lots from Sonnabend, Ashley Bickerton’s expansive wall relief Commercial Piece #3 (1990), covered with gallery and fashion-house logos and comprised of anodised aluminium, wood, leather, acrylic and rubber, sold for $120,000 ($153,600 with fees). Both the Lichtenstein and the Bickerton were backed by third-party guarantees.

Andy Warhol, Campbell's Soup Can (Turkey Noodle), 1962 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Recent findings suggest that price points for the Sonnabend trove zoomed higher with Andy Warhol’s iconicand hand painted Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle) (1962), which sold for $7.3m ($9m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. Another Lichtenstein, the painting Large Spool (1963)—a razor-sharp depiction of the titular object that has been featured in multiple gallery and museum exhibitions—squeaked by on the tails of a third-party guarantee at $7m ($8.6m with fees) against an ambitious estimate of $10m to $15m.

In a recent development, still in the Sonnabend lots, Jeff Koons’s toy-like Hulk (Friends) (2004-12), in polychromed bronze and standing nearly 6ft tall, found a newly introduced home for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees). And another Warhol, redolent with Hollywood celebrity, The Kiss (Bela Lugosi) (1963) in silkscreen ink on white paper, sold to another telephone bidder for $3.3m ($4.6m with fees).

Recent findings suggest that A petite Jasper Johns oil painting on cardboard, Numbers (1957), measuring just 8.5in by 6in and rich in shades of grey, made $2.6m ($3.2m with fees). It was featured in the artist’s first solo exhibition at the Leo Castelli Gallery in 1958. Ileana Sonnabend acquired it from the Castelli Gallery in 1959, the same year of her divorce from Leo Castelli.

The Sonnabend group of 19 lots, including three examples of key 20th-century French decorative art—among them a Jean Prouvé Trapéze table from around 1956 that hit $1.3m ($1.6m with fees)—all in tallied $33.3m ($41.9m with fees), compared to Christie’s pre-sale expectations for the group of $35m to $55m.

It has been revealed that illustrious consignor names continued with works from the collection of the late Museum of Modern Art trustee and patron Agnes Gund sold to benefit the Gund Art Foundation. They included Robert Ryman’s immaculate, small, square all-over white composition Untitled (1961), which brought $2.9m ($3.6m with fees). Vija Celmins’s photorealist oil painting Untitled (Ocean) (1990), which featured in the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s traveling retrospective in 2018-2020, went for $5.7m ($7.1m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. It also was backed by a third-party guarantee.

Vija Celmins, Untitled (Ocean), 1990 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Recent findings suggest that gund acquired Alexander Calder’s hanging metal mobile The Eye in the Black (1963) from the Perls Galleries in Fresh York in in 1967. On Thursday night it went to an online bidder for $2.8m ($3.5m with fees). Cindy Sherman’s Untitled Film Still #5 (1977), also widely exhibited and written about by major critics, sold for $320,000 ($409,6000 with fees). Gund had acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in November 2000 for a hammer price of $75,000.

Gund’s contemporary taste bordered on the encyclopaedic, as evidenced by an early Robert Rauschenberg work, Untitled (Gold Painting) (1953), in gold leaf on fabric and paper collage on canvas. The diminutive work, at 8in by 8in, fetched a sizeable sum, $1.7m ($2.1m with fees). Gund acquired it at Sotheby’s in Fresh York in May 1994 for a $55,000 hammer price.

A modestly scaled Lichtenstein work on paper in coloured pencil, graphite and paper collage, Artist’s Studio with Model (Study) (1974), sold to the art adviser Ralph DeLuca for $950,000 ($1.2m with fees).

Jim Nutt, Loom, 1999 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

In a recent development, A standout from the Gund trove, a work she described as “my Mona Lisa”, was another modestly-scaled work, by Jim Nutt, founder of Chicago’s Hairy Who group. Titled Loom (1999) and measuring 15in by 14in, the portrait of a woman with a penetrating gaze set a newly introduced auction record for Nutt’s work when it more than doubled its high estimate of $350,000 and ultimately sold for $850,000 ($1m with fees). The ten lots sold to benefit Gund’s charitable foundation tallied $20.3m ($25.7m with fees), squarely within Christie’s pre-sale estimate of $16m to $24m.

Though not part of the Gund Art Foundation offerings, Alice Neel’s double portrait David and Catherine Saalfield (1982) hailed from Agnes Gund’s family and brought $1.6m ($2m with fees). Gund acquired it directly from the artist the year it was painted—not surprising since the sitters were her young adult children.

Alice Neel, David and Catherine Saalfield, 1982 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

The appeal of buying a piece of the legacy of storied dealers and collectors did not fare so well for a work that had belonged to the late gallerist Marian Goodman. Bidding on Gerhard Richter’s Abstraktes Bild (1990) stalled at $5.7m, against an estimate of $6m to $8m, and the lot failed to sell. As Richter’s longtime Newly introduced York dealer, Goodman acquired the lushly surfaced squeegee painting directly from the artist and exhibited the painting in a gallery group show the year it was made. (A second Richter from another consignor fared better, with that somewhat larger Abstraktes Bild from 1991 bringing $7.6m, or $9.4m with fees.).

Among the works from more anonymous consignors, Richard Prince’s famous Nurse series made a splash when Everglade Nurse (2003), executed in acrylic and inkjet print on canvas, sold for $3.1m ($3.9m with fees). It last sold at Sotheby’s Fresh York in November 2008 for $3.4m with fees, a rather flat return after 18 years.

Recent findings suggest that large-scale paintings destined to test living room wall space were also in evidence with Christopher Wool’s untitled black-and-white abstraction from 2009, measuring more than 8ft tall. It brought $2m ($2.5m with fees). George Condo’s more than 9ft-wide Double Heads in Blue and Silver (2014), realised $2.4m ($3m with fees). The Condo hailed from the collection of Stefan Edlis and his wife Gael Neeson, who donated 44 works cumulatively valued at more than $400m to the Art Institute of Chicago in 2015.

The top lot of the evening, unsurprisingly, was Jean-Michel Basquiat’s quirky and text-rich composition, Untitled (Leonardo and his Five Grotesque Heads) (1983), which hammered to another anonymous telephone bidder for $28m ($32.8m with fees) against a sky-high estimate of $30m to $50m.

Jean-Michel Basquiat, Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads), 1983 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Evidently inspired by Leonardo da Vinci’s 1493 pen-and-ink drawing on paper A man tricked by Gypsies (also known as Five grotesque heads), from the Royal Collection Trust at Windsor Castle in London, Basquiat’s freestyle interpretation in oil stick and acrylic against a burnt orange background crackles with the artist’s terse way with wordplay and actually features eight heads in all.

Measuring 80in by 80in, the painting has no exhibition history, at least none acknowledged in Christie’s online catalogue entry—though it was included in the Whitney Museum of American Art’s 1992 Basquiat retrospective. The catalogue entry for the Whitney exhibition listed the owner as Zurich’s Bruno Bischofberger, an early and key champion of the artist. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s London in October 2005, when it was the top lot at £736,000 ($1.3m) including fees against an estimate of £400,000 to £600,000. Sotheby’s at the time identified the buyer as “US Trade” and the current consignor acquired it from that entity in 2006.

Julia Jo, One Fell Swoop, 2026 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

The evening ended on a sweet note with Julia Jo’s large-scale abstraction One Fell Swoop (2026), donated to benefit the Latest York-based Coalition for the Homeless. It set a new auction record for Jo’s work, fetching $320,000 ($409,600 with fees). (The night’s other new auction record was for the work of the Spanish artist Antonio Santín.).

Apart from that feeling, the outlook was not as rosy. “It’s been a very long week, with a lot of art, and I think people are tired,” DeLuca stated. “The theme of the week is that estimates are a little aspirational.”.

The long week’s last burst of activity will be a pair of day sales at Christie’s on Friday (20 November), after which the US art industry will mark a pause to observe Thanksgiving before migrating south for Art Basel Miami Beach.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Association of Photographers (AOP) has revealed the 36 finalists for its 2026 AOP Open Awards, a competition celebrating still and moving images by professional and amateur photographers from around the world.

Now in its 20th year, the competition allows photographers of all experience levels to compete on equal terms. Sponsored by Capture One, Fujifilm UK, and Maxima, this year’s awards are divided into three formats: single image, series, and moving image.

The finalists’ work will be exhibited at Fujifilm House of Photography in London from January 29 to March 14, 2027. The Gold and Silver winners will be announced at a private viewing on the evening of January 28.

It has been revealed that the Best in Show winner will receive £1,250 ($1,600), while the Gold and Silver winners will take home £250 and £100, respectively. Additional prizes from the sponsors and AOP membership are also on offer.

The 36 shortlisted works cover a wide range of subjects, from LGBTIQ+ communities in the remote jungles of Suriname to Muslim women competing in Tbourida, an equestrian sport with roots in 16th-century battle tactics.

Other projects explore the tradition of workers, local clubs, and Sunday league teams playing football on London’s Hackney Marshes, alongside images of the game being played away from conventional pitches in Morocco. Elsewhere, photographers document the 40,000 Elvis impersonators and fans who descend on Porthcawl, a small seaside town in South Wales, for the world’s largest Elvis Presley festival.

The finalists also include a portrait of a woman continuing to run her family’s flower business in Kyiv throughout the war in Ukraine, portraits of national treasures David Hockney and Dame Judi Dench, and a visual ode to gratitude for skin.

All 36 finalist projects can be viewed on the AOP Awards website.

Recent findings suggest that the AOP Open Awards accept entries without categories or prescribed themes, leaving photographers free to submit work that is either personal or commissioned. The competition welcomes still photography, moving images, and creative uses of technology and innovation in work produced by a person. AI-generated images are not accepted, and all entries must have been created on or after January 1, 2025.

Tech Report: DxO Year in Review 2026: Four New Versions and Where Each One Fits in Your Edit

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A lot changed in DxO’s photo editing tools in 2026.
  • Together, DxO’s software updates changed how a hard file gets edited, from first cleanup to finished look.
  • Full disclosureThis article was brought to you by DxO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A lot changed in DxO’s photo editing tools in 2026. The strongest noise reduction reached far more cameras. Masks learned to find each person in a frame, and the distance behind them, without a brush. The glow of film around a streetlight went from a stack of layers to a single filter.

Together, DxO’s software updates changed how a hard file gets edited, from first cleanup to finished look.

Full disclosureThis article was brought to you by DxO. DxO’s Black Friday prices apply to new licenses and upgrades of PhotoLab 10, Nik Collection 9, ViewPoint 6, PureRAW 6 and FilmPack 8 through November 29. The prices are applied automatically at dxo.com/bf26/PetaPixel, with no code required.

Photos taken in Upcoming Mexico by Chris Niccolls and Michael Bonocore, in Cuba and Morocco by Michael Bonocore, and the Milky Way by Matt Suess.

Recent findings suggest that dxO released newly introduced versions of four applications in 2026: PureRAW 6, Nik Collection 9, PhotoLab 10 and, in October, ViewPoint 6. DxO keeps improving its applications, and three of them received free updates in November.

Each one handles a different stage of an edit. PureRAW cleans the RAW file, the unprocessed data a camera’s sensor records. PhotoLab develops that file into a share-worthy photograph, ViewPoint corrects perspective and distortion, and Nik Collection adds the finishing look.

In a recent development, always looking for upcoming ways to edit old photos, I ran photos from New Mexico, Cuba and Morocco through three of them for PetaPixel stories throughout 2026. Even though I also shoot astrophotography, a fourth story followed OM SYSTEM ambassador Matt Suess through a Milky Way edit, as he is a much more impressive editor than I am. What follows runs in the order of a typical edit of mine, and that starts before any creative decision, with the RAW file itself.

If you zoom to 100% on a frame shot at a high ISO, the camera’s sensitivity setting, the flaws become obvious. There is grainy noise in the shadows, edges the lens left soft and a dust spot or two from the sensor. Every later editing adjustment that you add only makes the problems worse, and they follow the photograph through the rest of the edit.

PureRAW 6 helps to make all of these fixes. It applies noise reduction, lens corrections and dust removal to the RAW file before editing starts, then hands back a newly introduced file to edit. The usual choice for that file is a DNG, a format that keeps a RAW file’s editing flexibility. The original RAW file is never modified.

This year’s PureRAW 6 expanded the reach of DeepPRIME XD3, the stronger of PureRAW’s two noise reduction engines.

Recent findings suggest that in the past, it only worked with Fujifilm’s X-Trans sensors. It now works with Bayer sensors, the design used by Canon, Nikon, Sony and OM SYSTEM.

It has been revealed that the lens corrections are an especially strong feature of DxO software, starting with PureRAW. They test each supported camera and lens pairing in their own lab, and PureRAW applies that impressive data for the exact combination that made the photograph.

In a recent development, in this day and age with skyrocketing storage costs, PureRAW 6 shrinks the files with a new DNG option called High-Fidelity Compression. In one example, a 57.8MB RAW file becomes a 136MB DNG without compression and a 17.2MB DNG with it.

I have come to find that most photographers are like me, and they often shoot with less than spotless equipment. Luckily, dust spots are automatically detected and removed across a whole batch. And in PureRAW 6, batch edits finish quicker, because the processor prepares the next image while the graphics card renders the current one.

Recent findings suggest that for noise reduction, start with DeepPRIME 3 and switch to XD3 for high-ISO files, heavy crops and fine detail such as feathers and fur. XD3 takes roughly twice as long, though the gap narrows on newer graphics cards, and it can leave artifacts (visible processing errors) on smooth surfaces. For portraits and architecture, stay with DeepPRIME 3.

Industry observers note that if the processed file goes back to Lightroom, make sure to turn off its own lens corrections and noise reduction for that file. PureRAW has already applied both, and running them a second time doubles the correction and creates artifacts.

PureRAW fits a photographer who intends to keep editing in Lightroom, Photoshop or Capture One, because it only changes the file those editors receive. A photographer who would rather work in one application gets DxO’s processing inside PhotoLab 10, the organization’s all-in-one editor. The full walkthrough, with recommended starting values for each control, is in DxO PureRAW 6: The Ultimate Beginner’s Guide.

Brightening one face in a group photograph is a small change. Telling the software which pixels belong to that face is the slow part. The area an adjustment affects is called a mask, and building one by hand means painting an outline and then cleaning up its edges.

Recent findings suggest that photoLab 10 builds those masks itself, and my guide shows each one at work on my photographs from Morocco. Its AI Masks recognize the individual people in a photograph instead of treating the group as one subject. One easy step generates a separate mask for each selected person.

For portraits the masks go finer, selecting facial skin, eyes, teeth, lips or facial hair without a hand-painted outline.

In a recent development, no matter the subject matter, every photograph has depth, and the new Depth Masks select areas by how far they are from the camera. PhotoLab builds a depth map, a model of which parts of the scene are near and which are far, without needing depth data recorded in the file.

These masks utilize DxO’s own AI, which runs on the photographer’s own computer, so the masks work on an airplane or in a hotel with unreliable Wi-Fi. Additionally, for those concerned with privacy, this means that the photos are never sent to the cloud and stay local on their computer.

Industry observers note that an automatic mask is a starting point to refine. When one misses part of the subject, PhotoLab 10 lets you correct it instead of rebuilding it.

Industry observers note that their U Point technology selects pixels by comparing their color and brightness. The Control Brush applies that matching inside an area the photographer paints.

Recent findings suggest that color grading shifts the color of the shadows, midtones and highlights separately. PhotoLab 10 puts all three on a single wheel, with a Global control for the whole image.

In a recent development, with the three ranges selected, dragging one marker moves all of them and keeps the same distance between them. This allows for trying a different color direction without rebuilding the color grade.

Industry observers note that the free 10.3 patch, released in November, extends the masks to noise reduction. Each local adjustment, an edit confined to a masked area, can now use its own noise reduction engine. Reserve DeepPRIME XD3 for the subject, where it extracts the most detail, and let DeepPRIME 3 handle the rest of the frame.

Sources indicate that point a camera up at a building and its walls lean toward each other in the frame. That is a perspective problem, and no exposure or color control fixes it. ViewPoint 6 is the application to fix that: it corrects geometry, perspective and distortion.

Released in October, it adds AI masks to ReShape Fusion, the tool that reshapes part of a picture. A mask finds the outline of a subject, however complex its shape, and the correction mesh is built to match it.

The photographer sets how far the change carries into the rest of the picture. As before, the correction needs no forced crop.

The standalone app now opens RAW files directly. November’s 6.1 enhancement adds DNG export, so a RAW file corrected in ViewPoint can leave with its geometry fixed and continue in any editor that opens DNG files.

Saving and exporting are now separate. Save records the corrections for the next session, and Export produces the finished image.

Industry observers note that photographers miss the days when film made bright lights glow. Light passed through the film’s layers, bounced off the back and leaked in again, leaving a soft halo around streetlights and candle flames. A digital sensor records the same lights with crisp edges and no halo.

Sources indicate that rebuilding that glow in Photoshop means duplicating the image, blurring the copy, masking the highlights and blending the layers together. Nik Collection 9 does it with one filter. The suite is a set of plug-ins for Photoshop, Lightroom Classic, Affinity and PhotoLab, and every application in the suite can open the photo from inside one of those editors.

That filter, Halation, is one of three upcoming effects in version 9, each shown on my photographs from Cuba in my Nik Collection 9 guide. It works best on an image that already has strong highlights worth softening, such as a night cityscape or a backlit portrait.

Chromatic Shift copies the color offset of a misaligned printing press, the red edge on one side of a face and the blue-green shadow on the other. A subtle shift of that kind gives a portrait a retro, editorial feel. Using an AI mask can keep it off the eyes and lips.

It has been revealed that glass Effect distorts the frame as if it were shot through textured glass. On a portrait, the distortion can wrap the frame while an AI Object Mask keeps the face sharp.

The fresh Color Grading filter in Color Efex, one of the Nik Collection 9’s plug-ins, puts shadows, midtones, and highlights on one wheel. Two shortcuts move all three together: one shifts hue, the color the tones lean toward, and the other shifts saturation, how vivid that color is. It gives photographers who finish in Photoshop, Lightroom Classic or Affinity the single-wheel grading that PhotoLab 10 has built in.

In a recent development, eighteen blending modes now sit inside Color Efex and a second plug-in, Analog Efex. A blending mode sets how an effect mixes with the image beneath it. On the Halation filter, Multiply sinks the glow into the shadows for a darker image, while Soft Light keeps the glow and more of the original contrast.

Aim any of these effects at part of the frame with AI Object Masks and Depth Masks, which work in every plug-in.

Recent findings suggest that version 9.2, the November update, adds snapshots. A snapshot saves every edit made so far. Try a different look, then come back to the snapshot at any point in the session.

The patch also brings 18 new presets, or saved looks: six each for Color Efex, Analog Efex and Silver Efex.

Matt Suess has photographed dark skies for decades and leads astrophotography workshops in places such as Grand Teton National Park. One of the most challenging files he has edited came from a test.

He normally caps his Milky Way exposures at ISO 6400, but he wanted to test PureRAW, so he shot a nightscape at ISO 12,800 to see how far he could push it.

Industry observers note that sharpening or adding contrast to a noisy night file bakes the noise in, so Suess runs noise reduction before he develops the RAW file. He opens PureRAW’s Preview and Process mode, which reveals the controls first, because a night sky is where he wants to make those calls himself.

Sources indicate that XD3 is the stronger engine, but a star field is where Suess often skips it. That much processing can start to soften the stars themselves, so he picks DeepPRIME 3, and he treats it as a per-image call.

He keeps Lens Sharpness on Standard, since the Hard setting starts sharpening the noise along with everything else.

The develop pass in Lightroom stays restrained. Suess switches to a color profile built for landscapes in place of the flatter default, adds a little contrast and holds back on the other sliders. He treats this pass as the place to protect the sky’s real color, with the finishing touches saved for later.

The finish happens in the Nik Collection 9 plug-in Color Efex, with the same four filters in the same order on nearly every Milky Way photograph. ClearView lifts the faint gray haze that dulls a night photo, and Suess keeps it low so it does not outline the stars. Glamour Glow spreads a soft bloom of light from the brightest points.

In a recent development, remove Color Cast pulls one unwanted color out of the frame. Tonal Contrast raises contrast separately in the shadows, midtones and highlights, and he raises the midtones, where the structure of the Milky Way sits. Once the stack works, he saves it as a preset for the next photograph from his astrophotography session.

In a recent development, suess fine tunes the filters with two tools. A Color Mask, a local adjustment added inside a filter, selects one color across the whole frame. He uses it on air glow, the faint green tint that reveals in the sky on very dark nights.

An AI Object Mask points a filter at a single foreground element instead of the whole image.

In a recent development, he judges every move at 100%, not from the small preview. Each one gets a before and after comparison, and he looks for halos, the bright rings that too much contrast leaves around stars. Every step of the edit, with his settings, is in How to Turn a Flat, Noisy RAW Into a Finished Milky Way Photograph.

Some jobs cannot be done by developing a RAW file: a layered composite, added text, an object removed or replaced, detailed retouching. Those jobs need a pixel editor, software that changes the pixels of the picture directly.

It has been revealed that dxO unveiled a partnership with Affinity by Canva in September. Affinity runs on macOS and Windows and costs nothing beyond a free Canva account.

According to recent reports, photoLab 10 debuted without a direct Export to Affinity button, and PhotoLab 10.1 added it. With the 10.3 update, Affinity’s own .af files appear in PhotoLab’s library like JPEG and TIFF files.

It has been revealed that that makes a round trip possible. A photographer can develop a RAW file in PhotoLab, continue in Affinity with retouching, compositing or layout, then finish and export the result in PhotoLab. Changes saved in Affinity are visible in PhotoLab straight away, and PhotoLab’s own adjustments are stored separately and never change the Affinity document.

According to recent reports, nik Collection 9.2 connects from the other side by saving its work as an .af file. The file keeps the edited image and the original as separate layers, and the masks come across as layers too. Going the other way has a limit: Nik Collection opens an .af file with its layers merged into a single image.

DxO’s Black Friday prices cover new licenses and upgrades of their five applications through November 29th, 2026. They apply to purchases from dxo.com/bf26/PetaPixel for macOS and Windows, are applied automatically with no code required, and cannot be combined with any other offers.

According to recent reports, pureRAW 6 suits a photographer who wants cleaner files and aims to keep editing in Lightroom, Photoshop or Capture One. It is $99.99, down from $139.99. The upgrade from version 4 or 5 is $69.99, down from $89.99.

Industry observers note that photoLab 10 suits a photographer who wants one application for the whole edit, with DxO’s processing, the automatic masks and the Color Grading wheel in the same place. It is $199.99, down from $249.99. The upgrade from version 8 or 9 is $99.99, down from $129.99.

According to recent reports, nik Collection 9 suits a photographer who has an editor already and wants the finishing looks: film glow, color grading and blending modes without stacked layers. It is $149.99, down from $179.99. The upgrade from version 7 or 8 is $79.99, down from $99.99.

ViewPoint 6 corrects geometry, perspective and distortion, and version 6, released in October, adds an AI mask that fits a correction to the outline of a subject. It is $99.99, down from $129.99. The upgrade from version 5 is $69.99, down from $84.99.

Sources indicate that filmPack 8 recreates the look of classic film stocks from laboratory measurements of real film, and it includes a tool that prepares home-scanned negatives and slides for editing. It is $74.99, down from $149.99. The upgrade from version 7 is $49.99, down from $89.99.

Free trials of every DxO application are available from dxo.com. November’s 10.3, 9.2 and 6.1 updates are free for owners of PhotoLab 10, Nik Collection 9 and ViewPoint 6.

The most accessible, repeatable high-value hotel redemption in travel rewards.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Picture this: You've been grinding toward your FI number, optimizing every dollar, and you've accumulated a stash of Chase Ultimate Rewards points sitting in your account. Now imagine checking into a clean, comfortable Hyatt Place in a city you're visiting for a wedding, a family reunion, or a long weekend — and the front desk agent hands you your keycard while your account balance drops by exactly 5,000 points. Not $150. Not $180. Five thousand points that you earned by buying groceries. That's the Category 1 Hyatt sweet spot — and it's the single most accessible, repeatable, high-value redemption in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A standard night at a Hyatt Place or Hyatt House in a mid-size U.S. city routinely runs **$100–$200 per night** in cash. At 5,000 points per night, you're redeeming at **2–4 cents per point (CPP)** — a range that demolishes the standard 1 cent per point benchmark that most casual rewards users never surpass. At 4 CPP on a $200 night, you're getting four times the value of a simple cash-back card. Every. Single. Time. The pricing inefficiency here is structural, not accidental. World of Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** — meaning a Category 1 property costs 5,000 points whether it's a Tuesday in January or a Friday night during a sold-out college football weekend when cash rates are spiking. The loyalty program doesn't dynamically price awards the way airlines do. That fixed ceiling is your edge. For the ChooseFI community, this redemption isn't just good — it's foundational. It's the first sweet spot that proves the system works. Before you're ready to redeem 60,000 points for a business class flight to Tokyo, you need to feel what it's like to hand over a handful of points and walk into a hotel room that would have cost you real money. This is that moment. It builds the muscle memory, the confidence, and the conviction that travel rewards are real — and that you're playing the game correctly. This is where the journey starts.

According to recent reports, world of Hyatt consistently delivers the highest cents-per-point value of any major hotel loyalty program. While Hilton and Marriott have moved to dynamic pricing — where award costs fluctuate based on demand — Hyatt maintains a fixed award chart. This structural difference is your edge. A Category 1 property costs 5,000 points whether it is a quiet Tuesday in February or a sold-out homecoming weekend. Combined with Chase Ultimate Rewards transfer ratios (1:1 from Sapphire Reserve, 4:3 from Sapphire Preferred) and instant transfer speed, Hyatt redemptions are the single best use of UR points for hotel stays. The ChooseFI community considers this the entry point that proves the entire travel rewards system works.

The core insight behind this sweet spot is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt uses a fixed-price award chart, and Category 1 is priced at a floor that hasn't kept pace with rising hotel cash rates.

In a recent development, most hotel loyalty programs have moved to dynamic pricing — meaning award nights fluctuate with demand, just like cash rates. Marriott Bonvoy®, Hilton Honors™, IHG One Rewards — they've all largely eliminated fixed charts in favor of algorithms that squeeze more points out of you when demand is high. Hyatt has held the line on a fixed chart, and that stubbornness is your opportunity.

Sources indicate that the Category 1 floor sits at 5,000 points per night. As cash rates for qualifying properties have climbed with inflation — many now regularly pricing at $150–$200+ — the points cost has remained anchored. The gap between what the market charges and what Hyatt charges in points is widening in your favor every year. That's not a bug in the system. It's a feature you're uniquely positioned to exploit by understanding it.

This redemption is built on two of the best transferable points currencies available to everyday consumers:.

Recent findings suggest that both transfers are instant, which means you can search for availability before committing your points, confirm the room you want is bookable, and then initiate the transfer and complete the booking — all in one sitting. This is a critical distinction from some airline partners where transfers take 24–72 hours and you're transferring on faith. With Hyatt, there's no leap of faith required.

Recent findings suggest that the transfer ratio matters. With a Sapphire Reserve, every UR point becomes one Hyatt point — 15,000 UR points covers three Category 1 nights with zero waste. With a Sapphire Preferred, the 4:3 ratio means you need 20,000 UR points for the same 15,000 Hyatt points. Bilt transfers at 1:1.

Industry observers note that world of Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges on award bookings. This matters more for higher-tier redemptions, but it's worth internalizing as a feature of the program overall. When you book 5,000 points for a hotel night, that's your cost. You'll pay any applicable taxes at checkout — typically $10–$25 — but there are no program-imposed carrier fees or redemption surcharges eating into your value.

Hyatt's full chart runs from 3,500 points (Category 1 standard) up to 45,000 points (Category 8) per night. Understanding this structure helps you see the Category 1 sweet spot in context: it's the entry point, but it's not a consolation prize. Hyatt Place and Hyatt House properties are upper-midscale hotels — clean, well-maintained, often with free breakfast at Hyatt House locations and complimentary parking in suburban markets. These aren't budget motels. You're getting a genuinely comfortable night's sleep for points that most people have already earned without trying.

In a recent development, booking a Category 1 Hyatt award is one of the smoothest processes in all of travel rewards. Here's exactly how to do it from start to finish.

Filter further by selecting "Category 1–2" under the Points filter to swiftly surface the lowest-cost options. Availability is typically strong — Hyatt.com demonstrates real-time award inventory, and Category 1 properties almost always have rooms open. The booking window extends 395 days out, so you can plan well in advance for travel around a specific event.

Recent findings suggest that once you've found the property and dates you want, note the exact points cost displayed. For Category 1 properties, this should read 5,000 points per night. Add the room to your cart and proceed — but do not check out yet if your Hyatt account currently has zero balance.

In a recent development, open a fresh browser tab and navigate to your Chase Ultimate Rewards portal (chase.com/ultimaterewards) or Bilt dashboard. Select "Transfer to Travel Partners" and choose World of Hyatt from the list. Enter the number of points you need (5,000 per night, minimum), confirm your World of Hyatt membership number, and initiate the transfer.

Sources indicate that chase and Bilt transfers to Hyatt are instant. Note: Sapphire Reserve transfers at 1:1 while Sapphire Preferred transfers at 4:3 (4 UR = 3 Hyatt). Refresh your Hyatt account and your points will be there, ready to use.

According to recent reports, return to your Hyatt browser tab and complete the checkout process. Select "Redeem Points" as your payment method, confirm the points deduction matches what you expected, and finalize the reservation. You'll receive a confirmation email immediately.

If your preferred property shows no award availability on your dates, try these workarounds:.

Recent findings suggest that go to hyatt.com and use the "Points + Cash" or "Use Points" search filter. Category 1 properties will display at 5,000 points per night. You can also browse by category directly — look for Hyatt Place and Hyatt House locations in secondary cities and suburban markets.

Sources indicate that always verify that your desired dates show award availability before initiating a transfer from Chase or Bilt. While transfers are instant, confirming availability first ensures you never have orphaned points sitting in your Hyatt account with no immediate use.

Sources indicate that once the points land in your Hyatt account, complete the booking through hyatt.com or the World of Hyatt app. You will pay applicable taxes at checkout (typically $10 to $25 per night) but no additional redemption fees.

Recent findings suggest that before booking, note the cash rate for the same room and dates. Divide the cash rate by 5,000 to calculate your cents per point. If a room costs $150 per night and you are paying 5,000 points, you are getting 3 cents per point — triple the baseline 1 cent per point cash back value.

#80098. Latest Update: The Mothers Saving Borneo: Fighting Fire, Patriarchy, and Super El Niño
