#80073. Layered Compositions Will Level Up Your Landscape Photography

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2992 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Petapixel ↗ Open Full Page

Layered Compositions Will Level Up Your Landscape Photography

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2992 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A landscape can look dramatically different in person than it does in a photograph, particularly when a scene loses its sense of depth and scale.
  • Industry observers note that creating depth in landscape photography starts with understanding how different parts of a scene relate to one another.
  • Getting those elements to work together takes more than placing an interesting subject in the foreground or pointing the camera at a dramatic mountain range.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A landscape can look dramatically different in person than it does in a photograph, particularly when a scene loses its sense of depth and scale. Explore how thoughtful layering brings distant views to life by connecting nearby details with the features that make a location memorable.

Industry observers note that creating depth in landscape photography starts with understanding how different parts of a scene relate to one another. Foreground details establish scale, middle-ground features connect the viewer to the wider landscape, and distant elements provide context. When these elements complement one another, they give the photograph greater dimension and draw the viewer through the frame.

Getting those elements to work together takes more than placing an interesting subject in the foreground or pointing the camera at a dramatic mountain range. Camera position, focal length, overlapping shapes, and changing light all influence how layers appear and how easily the viewer can distinguish them. This guide explores how to apply these techniques in the field—from recognizing natural layers and arranging them within the frame to avoiding visual clutter.

Sources indicate that the foundation of a layered landscape composition is the relationship between its foreground, middle ground, and background. These three zones provide a visual structure that communicates distance and gives the viewer a sense of moving through the scene. The foreground is the area closest to the camera, the middle ground occupies the space between the viewer and the distant scenery, and the background typically contains the farthest elements, such as mountains, hills, or the sky.

According to recent reports, each layer serves a distinct purpose. The foreground anchors the immediate setting and gives the viewer an entry point. The middle ground bridges that starting point to the rest of the landscape, while the background provides context, scale, and a sense of distance. When these elements work together, the photograph feels far more dimensional than a composition built around a single distant subject.

Not every landscape needs three clearly defined layers. A photograph of a mountain reflected in a lake, for example, might rely on two dominant planes, while a forest scene could contain several overlapping layers of trees. The goal is not to force every scene into a rigid formula, but to recognize the distinct planes of distance within it and decide how each contributes to the composition.

Before setting up the camera, take a moment to identify what occupies each part of the view. Look for elements that naturally lead the eye through the frame, as well as areas that might compete for attention. Taking this step helps determine whether the scene already has a strong visual structure or whether changing your position could reveal a more effective arrangement.

It has been revealed that A strong foreground gives a landscape photograph an immediate point of entry. Rocks, grasses, wildflowers, fallen trees, shoreline details, and other nearby features establish a sense of place while making the distance feel more pronounced. Rather than simply filling the bottom of the frame, the foreground should serve a clear purpose in the composition.

Look for foreground elements that relate to the larger scene. A line of rocks leading toward a mountain, a patch of wildflowers beneath a distant ridgeline, or a weathered tree framing a valley can connect the viewer to the landscape beyond. These details establish scale and make an expansive scene feel more tangible.

Camera position has a considerable effect on how prominent the foreground becomes. Lowering the camera gives nearby objects greater visual weight, often exaggerating their apparent size relative to the background. This can create a dramatic sense of depth, particularly when using a wide-angle lens. However, getting too close can make a foreground object overwhelm the rest of the photograph. Move the camera forward and backward while checking how much space the foreground occupies and whether it remains connected to the distant view.

Recent findings suggest that pay attention to the edges of the frame as well. A partially cropped rock, branch, or other object along the border can look accidental if it draws attention without adding to the composition. Sometimes shifting the camera just a few inches is enough to position the foreground more deliberately. If there is no suitable foreground element, resist the urge to include something merely to fill the space. A clean, uncomplicated foreground is often more effective than one that distracts from the landscape.

The middle ground is often the most overlooked part of a landscape composition. Photographers frequently concentrate on finding an interesting foreground and capturing a dramatic background, leaving the space between them without a clear visual role. Yet this middle zone is essential because it bridges near and distant elements, helping the photograph feel cohesive.

Recent findings suggest that middle-ground subjects can include rolling hills, tree lines, rivers, fields, valleys, waterfalls, or clusters of rocks. These features smooth the transition between planes of distance and can create a natural path through the image. A river winding between a foreground shoreline and distant mountains, for example, gives the viewer a route through the landscape. A series of hills can create successive bands that gradually recede toward the horizon.

Look for shapes and lines that link different parts of the scene. A sloping hillside might echo the angle of a nearby rock formation, while a line of trees could guide attention toward a distant peak. Repeating forms also help unify a composition; a series of ridges or tree-covered slopes creates a visual rhythm that reinforces depth.

Recent findings suggest that if the middle ground feels empty, consider whether changing your position reveals more of the landscape between the foreground and background. Moving laterally along a trail or shoreline can shift the relationship between overlapping features and expose details that were previously hidden. You may also find that a slightly longer focal length brings distant layers together more effectively, especially in landscapes with repeating hills or ridgelines.

According to recent reports, the background gives a landscape its broader context, but distant elements can easily lose definition when they blend together. A mountain peak that merges with a similarly toned ridge, for example, may lose its shape and visual impact. Creating separation between background features preserves their individual forms and reinforces the sense of distance.

Light and weather often provide natural separation. Sidelighting reveals the contours of distant mountains, while low-angle sunlight casts alternating bands of brightness and shadow across hillsides. Fog, mist, and atmospheric haze also distinguish successive layers by reducing contrast as the landscape recedes. These conditions produce subtle tonal transitions that make distant features appear farther away.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra).

It has been revealed that camera position matters, too. A slight change in elevation or angle can separate a mountain from the ridge behind it or reveal a gap between two overlapping peaks. Before taking the photograph, examine the outlines of distant features and look for places where they merge. Moving even a short distance can create enough separation to make the shapes easier to read.

Exposure also affects how well those details are retained. Bright skies behind dark mountains often create a wide dynamic range, particularly at sunrise and sunset. Check the histogram and highlight warnings to avoid losing important sky detail. If necessary, use exposure bracketing or a graduated neutral density filter to manage the difference in brightness. Preserving tonal detail across the scene helps maintain the distinction between distant layers.

In a recent development, overlap is one of the most direct ways to communicate depth in a landscape photograph. When one object partially obscures another, the viewer immediately recognizes that the two elements occupy different planes of distance. A foreground tree overlapping a distant ridge, for example, creates a clear spatial relationship even though the photograph is a two-dimensional image.

It has been revealed that look for natural arrangements where landscape features overlap cleanly. Successive mountain ridges, layers of trees, and rolling hills are particularly useful because they provide repeated shapes at different distances. The viewer can follow these forms as they recede into the background, creating a sense of depth without requiring a prominent foreground subject.

Industry observers note that how much elements overlap also matters. If one element completely hides another, the relationship between them becomes less obvious. If the objects barely touch, their outlines can merge into an awkward visual intersection. Small changes in camera position can reveal more of one feature or create a cleaner separation between them.

This is especially vital when photographing forests or densely layered landscapes. Branches and tree trunks can easily intersect in ways that make the image feel tangled. Rather than trying to include every interesting tree, look for openings where individual trunks and branches remain distinguishable. A slight shift to the left or right may separate one tree from another and make the overall arrangement easier to read.

Focal length directly influences how distance and scale appear in the finished photograph. Wide-angle lenses are useful when the foreground is an important part of the composition. Their broad field of view captures nearby details alongside distant scenery, while perspective exaggeration between close and far objects emphasizes depth.

When using a wide-angle lens, foreground placement becomes particularly vital. An object close to the camera can appear much larger than everything behind it, sometimes dominating the frame. This can be effective when the foreground has a strong shape or texture, but it can also make the composition feel unbalanced. Pay attention to how close you are to the nearest subject and whether its scale supports the relationship between layers.

Telephoto lenses offer a different approach. Rather than emphasizing the distance between foreground and background, longer focal lengths narrow the field of view and make distant features appear closer together. This visual compression can emphasize repeated layers of mountains, hills, trees, or other landscape elements. A scene that looks relatively open through a wide-angle lens may reveal a more graphic arrangement when photographed with a telephoto lens.

It has been revealed that neither approach is inherently better. A wide-angle lens communicates the scale of an expansive landscape, while a telephoto lens isolates a series of distant forms and emphasizes their relationship. If a scene has several interesting layers, try photographing it at different focal lengths before deciding which version best captures the scene.

In a recent development, light makes layered landscapes more distinctive by revealing shapes, textures, and tonal differences across planes of distance. The same scene may look relatively flat under even midday light but become far more dimensional when low-angle sunlight creates alternating bands of illumination and shadow.

Sidelighting is particularly useful for emphasizing the contours of hills, mountains, and other landforms. As the sun sits low on the horizon, ridges catch the light while valleys remain in shadow. This creates visual separation between successive layers and gives the scene a stronger sense of form. Backlighting can also be effective, especially when photographing trees, grasses, or other translucent elements in the foreground.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra).

Recent findings suggest that atmospheric conditions provide another way to distinguish distance. Mist and fog soften the contrast of distant hills and mountains, creating a series of progressively lighter layers. After a storm, breaks in clearing clouds often spotlight individual sections of a landscape while leaving others in shadow. These changing conditions produce natural divisions between foreground, middle ground, and background without requiring strong compositional elements in every part of the frame.

When photographing in changing weather, be prepared to work quickly. Use a tripod when shutter speeds are slow, but avoid relying on one fixed composition if the light is moving across the scene. Take multiple exposures as conditions evolve, particularly when sunlight briefly strikes a distant ridge or a break in the clouds reveals a new layer. These short-lived lighting conditions can make a substantial difference to the finished image.

Industry observers note that adding layers can create depth, but it can also introduce too much visual information. A foreground full of rocks, a middle ground crowded with trees, and a background filled with overlapping mountain peaks may leave the viewer unsure where to look. The challenge is deciding which elements contribute to the photograph and which ones make it harder to read.

Start by identifying the primary subject or visual feature. This does not have to be a single object — it might be a mountain range, a winding river, or a series of repeating ridgelines. Once you know what should attract attention, consider whether the other layers support it. A foreground element that pulls the eye away from the main subject may need to be repositioned or excluded from the frame.

Industry observers note that simplifying a composition does not always mean removing entire layers—it often means adjusting how much visual weight each one carries. A smaller foreground can establish context without competing with the background, while an open middle ground gives the viewer’s eye room to travel through the scene. Switching to a longer focal length can also help trim distracting edges or unrelated elements.

It has been revealed that watch for bright highlights, stray branches, and high-contrast objects that pull attention away from the subject. These distractions become more disruptive in a layered composition, where the viewer’s eye is already navigating multiple planes. Scan the entire frame before pressing the shutter—paying close attention to the corners and edges—for anything that interrupts the visual flow. Often, shifting the camera slightly or tightening the crop is enough to clean up the frame.

In a recent development, even a minor shift in camera position can alter the relationship between every layer in a landscape. Moving forward or backward changes the scale and placement of foreground objects, while stepping laterally can reveal or conceal distant features. Camera height also dictates how much of the ground plane is visible and how smoothly the foreground transitions into the background.

Rather than immediately setting up a tripod at the first scenic overlook, take time to explore the area. Walk along a ridge, follow a shoreline, or look for a slightly elevated vantage point that opens up the landscape. Observe how foreground elements align with distant peaks, trees, or ridges. Often, the strongest composition sits just a few steps away from the obvious viewpoint.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra).

According to recent reports, once you find a promising spot, a tripod helps you fine-tune height and framing deliberately. Lowering the tripod emphasizes nearby textures, while raising it reveals more of the middle ground. If your tripod has an adjustable center column, extend it sparingly as raising the column too high reduces stability, especially in windy conditions.

Perspective control is also worth considering in scenes with strong vertical lines. Tilting the camera upward causes trees, cliffs, or buildings to converge toward the top of the frame. While that converging effect can work creatively, keeping vertical lines straight requires leveling the camera and adjusting your composition by stepping back or switching to a wider lens. What matters most is whether the perspective reinforces how you want the layers to relate.

Recent findings suggest that building a layered landscape composition becomes much easier when you approach a scene methodically. Start by identifying the anchor of the view—whether that is a distant peak, a line of trees, a winding river, or light sweeping across a valley. From there, work backward toward the camera to see which nearby elements can serve as an entry point without overpowering the main subject.

Once you have identified potential layers, move around to test different arrangements. Look for foreground features that lead naturally into the middle ground, and check how distant shapes overlap. Watch the gaps between objects so unrelated elements do not merge into awkward outlines. If the scene feels overly busy, simplify with a tighter framing or a longer focal length rather than trying to include everything.

It has been revealed that your camera settings should support both the field conditions and the intended depth of the photograph. For a static landscape requiring front-to-back sharpness, a mid-range aperture such as f/8 or f/11 is a reliable starting point. Focus roughly one-third of the way into the scene, then zoom in on your review screen to verify that both the nearest and farthest key elements are sharp. Optimal focus distance depends on focal length, aperture, and proximity to the foreground; if a very close foreground and distant background cannot both be rendered sharply in a single frame, focus stacking is a reliable alternative when the scene is still.

Industry observers note that keep your ISO low when practical, but do not let the pursuit of a noise-free file force an overly slow shutter speed. Wind moving through grasses or foliage often calls for a faster exposure, even if that requires raising your ISO. A tripod eliminates camera shake, but it cannot freeze motion within the landscape itself.

Sources indicate that before leaving a location, photograph the scene using several different focal lengths and compositions. Start with a wider frame that emphasizes the foreground, then try a tighter composition that compresses repeating layers or gives greater weight to the background. I also like revisiting locations under different light and weather, as shifts in atmosphere or time of day can completely transform a scene’s character and yield a more dramatic photograph. Comparing these variations helps reveal which arrangement and conditions best capture the landscape.

According to recent reports, ultimately, layered landscape photography is about building intentional relationships between elements in a scene. Foreground, middle ground, and background offer a reliable structural framework, but their impact depends on how well they connect, overlap, and remain visually distinct. By paying close attention to camera position, focal length, light, and visual balance, you can create landscapes with genuine depth and clarity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world? The latest Art Basel & UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 report, which surveyed 3,100 high net-worth individuals (HNWIs) who collect art, reveals that social media platforms—and Instagram in particular—are an increasingly important tool for discovering art and artists, buying works and promoting collections. Here is how online platforms are being used and what the art world can learn from it.

Industry observers note that while the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media. Interestingly, online channels were a less common route into collecting for Gen Z collectors (10%) than for Gen X (16%), “running against any assumption that younger collectors might be more likely to find their way to collecting through digital channels”, the report states.

The data also shows that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas. “While being introduced to art through family or cultural exposure may reflect a more passive route into collecting, those who started out online were typically more active in seeking out art content,” the report says. “This suggests a more deliberate, self-directed collecting journey that carries forward into greater engagement with events later on.”.

When it comes to collecting, 58% of respondents stated they had used digital resources for advice with 32% of collectors citing either Instagram or X (formerly Twitter) as sources when it came to making purchases. Nineteen percent used recommendations from Instagram (up 2% year-on-year), including 22% of Gen Z respondents, and women were more likely to use them than men. The platform X—which has seen decreased usage in recent years due to controversies around its ownership and usage—was used by 18% of the sample, and this was again highest among Gen Z (23%).

A collectors’ likeliness to use social media recommendations for collecting also depended greatly on where a person was from: collectors in Hong Kong, the US and the UK were most likely to use social media for advice while those in Mainland China were less likely, undoubtedly due to the restrictions of social media platforms in the country.

Contrary to popular belief around the slow uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in the art world, the study also highlighted that collectors trusted AI tools for art recommendations twice as much as those from social media and influencers, and also slightly more than in-store advisors and editorial content.

The importance of ​​online and social media platforms in reaching collectors is growing. According to the survey, 27% of HNWIs’ total expenditure was made through such external platforms, up by 5 percentage points year-on-year and from 17% in 2024. The share of collectors buying directly from artists also grew to 69%, with 38% of works bought via Instagram, highlighting the benefits of a strong, independent social media presence for artists. It is also interesting to note that artist-direct spending through Instagram was higher among upcoming collectors than more experienced ones: 8% for those in the market for two years or less, versus just 2% for those collecting for 20 years or more.

But can seeing a work online really seal the deal? Apparently so—among the 75% of respondents who had purchased a work directly from a dealer in 2025/2026, 53% had bought via Instagram without viewing the work in person, up from 43% in 2024.

In a recent development, the report interestingly states that the youngest generation of collectors—Gen Z—are not the ones using social media the most in their collecting journeys. “The generation raised on social media is, it turns out, the one most inclined to keep its collecting close,” the report says. While the data showed that Gen Z were the highest-spending generation surveyed and had the most wide-ranging collecting habits, their awareness of digital footprints leads them to seek greater control and privacy over their "personal and cultural identities".

According to recent reports, “Anonymous accounts and smaller, niche social networking platforms allow them to communicate in ways that feel less pressurised and performative,” the report states. “With social media feeds heavily controlled and populated by algorithms rather than personal networks, Gen Z consumers are increasingly interested in taking back control over who sees their personal content by sharing it with smaller, vetted and carefully chosen audiences.”.

When it came to sharing information about their collections with the wider public, only 25% Gen Z shared their own content publicly, compared with 36% of millennials and around one third of other older collectors.

It has been revealed that within a broader FI travel strategy, this redemption pairs well with a Marriott Bonvoy® credit card for point accumulation and an Alaska Visa for direct mile earning. It's a medium-complexity move with a very high ceiling on value.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is honest. It's not complicated in concept, but it has two specific friction points that trip up even experienced travel rewards enthusiasts. **Challenge 1: Earning the Miles** Alaska Mileage Plan's isolation from major flexible currency programs (no Chase Ultimate Rewards, no Amex Membership Rewards, no Citi ThankYou transfers directly) means you can't simply funnel points you already have into Alaska. The primary path is the Alaska Airlines Visa (Bank of America) or a Marriott Bonvoy® conversion at an unfavorable 3:1 ratio. Plan your earning strategy well in advance. **Tip:** Prioritize the Alaska Visa signup bonus as your foundation, then supplement with Marriott points if needed. **Challenge 2: The Phone Booking Requirement** You cannot book this online. The call-in process intimidates people who've only ever booked travel digitally. **Tip:** Do your homework on ba.com first, have your dates ready, and approach the call as an informed customer — not someone asking for help finding availability. Agents respond well to specific, prepared callers. **Challenge 3: Cathay Award Availability** Cathay Pacific releases partner award space selectively and often in small quantities. Availability rated 3/5. **Tip:** Search exactly at the 331-day booking window, keep Qantas as your backup at the same price point, and be flexible with travel dates by even one or two days — a Tuesday departure often has inventory when Saturday doesn't. The good news: once you've done this once, you'll understand the system deeply enough to replicate it. The ChooseFI community has members who've booked this exact route multiple times. The first time takes effort. After that, it's a process you know cold.

According to recent reports, the fastest path is the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card from Bank of America, which typically offers a 60,000 to 75,000-mile sign-up bonus. That alone nearly covers the 55,000 miles needed. You can also transfer Marriott Bonvoy® points at 3:1 (165,000 Bonvoy points equals 55,000 Alaska miles) or earn miles through flying Alaska and its partners.

Yes. You would book two separate one-way awards at 55,000 miles each. You could fly Cathay Pacific one direction and Qantas the other, or mix carriers based on availability. Each one-way can include its own free stopover.

Cathay Pacific typically releases Business Class award space 90 to 330 days before departure. The sweet spot for finding availability is usually 90 to 120 days out, when airlines release unsold premium cabin seats. Check frequently, as availability can appear and disappear promptly.

Alaska allows one free stopover on one-way awards. On a routing from the US to Australia via Hong Kong, you can stop in Hong Kong for any number of days at no additional miles cost. Simply tell the agent when booking that you want a stopover in HKG. This effectively gives you two destinations for the price of one redemption.

Sources indicate that the Alaska Mileage Initiative redemption for Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class to Australia is one of the most extraordinary sweet spots in travel rewards. At 55,000 miles for a seat that costs $5,000 to $12,000 in cash — with zero fuel surcharges and a free stopover in Hong Kong — this redemption delivers 9 to 22 cents per point. It requires more planning and effort than a simple hotel booking, but the payoff is a genuine luxury travel experience that proves the asymmetric value the FI community builds its travel rewards strategy around.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Kodak SlideTag Is a $35 Blind-Box E Ink Photo Display and AirTag Alternative

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, reto, the tech giant behind the wildly successful Kodak Charmera, has announced its next blind box-style product: the Kodak SlideTag.
  • The SlideTag uses that E Ink display to allow users to upload their own photos into it and display them like single slides from the golden age of film.
  • Industry observers note that “When Kodak introduced Kodachrome in 1935, the slide mount promptly became the classic way people projected and shared their favorite memories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, reto, the tech giant behind the wildly successful Kodak Charmera, has announced its next blind box-style product: the Kodak SlideTag. It’s a small, color E Ink display with AirTag-like capability and a user-replaceable battery.

The SlideTag uses that E Ink display to allow users to upload their own photos into it and display them like single slides from the golden age of film.

Industry observers note that “When Kodak introduced Kodachrome in 1935, the slide mount promptly became the classic way people projected and shared their favorite memories. Families gathered around glowing projectors, watching their favorite moments illuminated inside a simple cardboard frame,” Reto states.

“Decades later, the Kodak SlideTag breathes new life into that iconic retro slide frame, bringing a vintage touch to the digital age. Designed as a miniature memory holder, it allows you to digitize your precious moments and easily carry your stories wherever you go.”.

In a recent development, the SlideTag measures 39.3(W) x 46(H) x 7.58(D) mm and weighs just 16.6 grams. The central display is 1.54 inches across with a resolution of 240 x 240 pixels. The color E Ink can display up to six colors and because E Ink doesn’t require any power to retain the image, the SlideTag can display a photo and retain other functionality for extended lengths of time without dying.

Industry observers note that the “other functionality” that does require battery power is the compatibility with Apple Find My and Google Android Find Hub. The IP54 rated keychain supports Bluetooth 5.4 and has a real-time tracking range of up to 30 meters while also being compatible with both Google and Apple’s tracking networks. The SlideTag can also buzz on command at 75 dB to help locate it.

It has been revealed that in addition to supporting photos, the SlideTay also comes with a host of other features such as a custom QR code for displaying social links or digital business cards. It can also display live daily to-do lists, calendars, event countdowns, or personalized name badges. Photos can be set as simple galleries that only change when the button on the back is double pressed or as slideshows that change as often as once per day. All of the features of the SlideTag require connecting to the Kodak Memory Link app.

Reto is offering the Kodak SlideTag in eight standard styles, with one extra secret design style that is substantially rarer than the others: a silver color.

All SlideTags come with a collectible 35mm slide frame that actually fits a real 35mm slide as well as other small collectibles.

The Kodak SlideTag is available starting today for $35 or as a box of eight for $280.

“We're not saying they're perfect” says architect fighting to save Melbourne's public housing blocks

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1521 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its initiative to demolish all of Melbourne’s public housing towers.
  • Confirmed by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne’s public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with new housing by 2051.
  • Officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Ben Hosking, Michael Pham.

Architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its initiative to demolish all of Melbourne’s public housing towers. In this interview, he sets out why he believes retrofit is the smarter approach.

Confirmed by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne’s public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with new housing by 2051.

Officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives. They claim the towers do not meet modern standards and cost too much to maintain, and that the redevelopment programme will triple housing capacity and improve the quality of homes.

But the policy has proved highly controversial, with critics particularly angry about a lack of transparency or consultation with residents, who are being relocated.

It is now subject to an ongoing legal dispute, has prompted concern from the UN’s special rapporteur on housing, and become a political concern in the build-up to the Victorian state election later this month.

Among the voices leading calls for a change of course is Melbourne not-for-profit research and design practice Office.

Office has worked pro bono to make the case for refurbishing the towers, after learning from residents that the government has not published feasibility studies for keeping any of the condemned estates.

“We thought that was pretty odd that you wouldn’t do a refurbishment study on these estates,” Office director Simon Robinson told Dezeen.

“So we took it upon ourselves to start to do these feasibility studies, along with public housing residents.”.

It has been revealed that “We’re not saying that they’re in perfect condition,” he added. “We’re also not saying that all of them should be refurbished – perhaps some are beyond repair. All we are saying is that these refurbishment studies need to occur.”.

In fact, feasibility studies have been conducted by the government but not been made public, despite requests by the Victorian Legislative Council.

By avoiding the relocation of residents, Office estimates that a retrofit and infill approach would cost around $300 million less than demolition and rebuild.

“As all the estates are occupied, the cost of relocating and housing the residents during construction work needs to be included in the project cost; this is consistently excluded and never disclosed,” said Robinson.

“We have estimated that these costs are very significant, with reports indicating that the government is spot purchasing or head-leasing properties from the private market.”.

The practice has put together a counter-proposal based on a strategy that it calls Retain Repair Reinvest (RRR).

RRR focuses on retaining buildings without displacing residents, carrying out renovation work to improve housing comfort and energy efficiency while reducing construction waste and carbon impact.

Robinson agrees that most of Victoria’s existing public housing buildings are currently not fit for purpose – buildings are rundown, cold in winter, and sweltering in summer. But he believes comfortable living standards can be achieved through renovations.

Office has applied its RRR strategy to three Melbourne estates in hypothetical case studies – Ascot Vale Estate, Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.

Formerly home to approximately 1,500 people, Flemington Estate’s four towers make up about 10 per cent of Victoria’s high-rise public housing stock.

Only about 32 households remain, though an injunction prevents Homes Victoria from serving further eviction notices while legal challenges are pending.

Office has proposed retaining the estate’s 720 dwellings and building an additional 577 infill social housing units to increase density.

Newly introduced facades and private balconies would be added, with other upgrades including integrated underground parking, a central communal green space, new heating and cooling systems, improved insulation, new kitchens and bathrooms.

According to recent reports, energy efficiency is another key focus. Double-glazed windows, photovoltaic cells, and water conservation systems would provide a 55 percent reduction of global warming potential compared to the demolition approach, according to Office.

Despite the seemingly obvious benefits, the Victorian government has so far been unmoved by the studies presented by the practice.

Robinson believes the reason lies in the fact that the state government no longer wants to manage public housing.

“When the state government manages public housing, they are responsible for maintaining the buildings and organising newly introduced tenants – all the admin that comes with owning a building,” he stated.

As well as the demolitions, also attracting concern is the type of housing proposed for redevelopment under the HRRP.

Rather than like-for-like public housing, the latest homes will be “community housing” – developed by private developers, and split between below-market and market-rate rental homes.

Despite still being classed as social housing by the state government, community housing is slightly more expensive, and the tenancy is less secure from eviction.

Robinson believes the term was created to misdirect the public.

“What they’re building is community housing, not public housing, so there’s no longer any public housing being rebuilt in Victoria,” he stated.

“The government is now calling everything social housing, because they don’t want the public to know that it’s no longer public housing,” he continued.

“Victoria has the lowest percentage of public housing stock in Australia, and we’re at the moment demolishing it all and turning it into private and community housing.”.

Sources indicate that the glitch is particularly charged in the context of Australia‘s housing-affordability crisis. There are at the moment over 60,000 people on the waitlist for social housing in Victoria, where social housing accounts for three per cent of all dwellings, below the national average of 4.2 per cent and the OECD average of 7 per cent.

“Public housing serves as foundational social infrastructure that treats shelter as an essential human right,” said Robinson.

“By offering rents permanently capped to income and delivering unmatched security of tenure, it provides an unconditional safety net for society’s most vulnerable households.”.

Office’s work has gained political attention. In November 2023, the Victorian Legislative Council debated the merits of the RRR approach, with the council’s Legal and Social Challenges Committee urging the government to reconsider demolition and explore all refurbishment options.

According to recent reports, the team can already claim a small victory. At Ascot Vale Estate, the first RRR case study released by Office, the development was quietly removed from the planned demolitions list on the Homes Victoria website and part of the estate has since been refurbished.

The estate is a collection of 57 three-storey brick housing blocks, built in 1947 and designed by renowned modernist architect and public housing advocate Best Overend during his time with the Housing Commission.

This gave Robinson and his team hope that the government would consider the alternatives if presented with the option.

“We have presented to Homes Victoria, we’ve presented to different ministers as well, and we’ve kind of heard that they are starting to look at retrofit some of their existing building stock,” stated Robinson.

“It kind of suggests that perhaps they’re gonna prefer we show all of them. So we released the following studies on Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.”.

However, Barak Beacon Estate has since been demolished, and the construction of the redevelopment is due to complete by the end of the year.

Now the fate of Flemington Tower awaits a ruling from the High Court of Australia following a hearing last month.

A class action filed by Inner Melbourne Community Legal on behalf of public housing residents in North Melbourne and Flemington is on its last appeal, after the Supreme Court of Victoria and Victorian Court of Appeal ruled in favour of demolition.

Meanwhile, the Liberal opposition has pledged to pause the HRRP if it wins office at the upcoming state election.

Robinson hopes he and his team have done enough, and continue to raise awareness about the concern.

“We’ve gotten to a point where we feel we can’t just keep putting out these reports,” he mentioned.

“The papers we produced are quite dense and not for the general public. So what we’re now doing is translating that work into a series of publications, putting it in bookshops, and making it more accessible for the general public.”.

It has been revealed that “We continue interviews with different residents, different advocates, different professionals, speaking with journalists and doing lectures. The idea is to bring awareness to what’s occurring, rather than us doing more reports.”.

He is also calling for a frank discussion in the architecture community about the redevelopment projects, which many of Australia’s prominent studios are working on.

“All the significant-name architects are working on these estate renewals, some have even won awards as exemplar projects for these architects to promote their practice in terms of doing public good,” stated Robinson.

Industry observers note that “It’s really hard to find anyone who’s willing to talk about why they’re doing it, or is it good, the displacement and environmental issues. We’re alone.”.

Dezeen put Robinson’s claims to the Victorian state government, but was told it could not respond in the lead-up to the election.

Photography by Ben Hosking, Michael Pham.
